topic: RAG versus fine tuning versus long context
q: What is retrieval augmented generation, and why does it work?
plain: RAG means the system looks up relevant text first and then lets the language model answer using that text. A model on its own answers from what it memorised during training, like a person answering from memory. RAG hands it the right pages first, like an open book exam. For example, the original 2020 RAG paper built one index from Wikipedia as of 2016 and another from 2018: with the matching index the model answered about 70 percent of questions about world leaders correctly, with the wrong one only 4 to 12 percent. Swapping the index changed what the model knew without any retraining.
deep: Lewis et al. (NeurIPS 2020) frame it as combining **parametric memory** (knowledge in the weights) with **non parametric memory** (an external index). Their model: a DPR retriever (two BERT base encoders) over 21M Wikipedia passages of 100 words, and a 400M parameter BART generator, trained end to end on the query encoder and generator with the document encoder and index frozen. RAG-Sequence marginalises over the top K documents per output sequence, $p(y|x) \approx \sum_{z} p_\eta(z|x) \prod_i p_\theta(y_i|x,z,y_{<i})$; RAG-Token marginalises per token. It set the state of the art on open Natural Questions (44.5 exact match). Index hot swapping: 70 percent (2016 index, 2016 leaders) and 68 percent (2018 index, 2018 leaders) versus 12 and 4 percent with mismatched indexes. Why it works: knowledge becomes inspectable, updatable and citable, and the model conditions on evidence instead of recall.
say: RAG means retrieving relevant passages at question time and conditioning the model's answer on them. The original paper described it as pairing the model's parametric memory, what's in the weights, with non parametric memory, an index you can edit. The experiment I like is index swapping: with a 2016 Wikipedia index the model got about seventy percent of 2016 world leader questions right, and with a mismatched index it dropped to single digits. So you can update what the system knows by changing the index, no training, and you know exactly which passage supported each answer.
must_mention: index can be updated without training
answers can cite the passage used

followups.q: What did the original RAG model use as retriever and generator?
followups.a: DPR with BERT base encoders over 21M Wikipedia passages, and BART large as generator.

followups.q: What is the difference between RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token?
followups.a: Sequence uses the same retrieved document for the whole answer; Token can draw on a different document for each token.

traps: Describing RAG as just pasting search results into a prompt with no thought about retrieval quality.

topic: RAG versus fine tuning versus long context
q: When would you use RAG and when would you fine tune?
plain: Use RAG when the model needs facts, especially facts that change, that you must cite, or that differ by user. Use fine tuning when you need the model to behave differently: follow a format, adopt a tone, or get good at a narrow task. A customer support bot should retrieve the current refund policy rather than be trained on it, because the policy will change next month. But teaching the same bot to always answer in a fixed JSON format is a fine tuning job. The two combine well: retrieval for knowledge, fine tuning for behaviour.
deep: Facts in weights have no provenance, cannot be scoped per user, cannot be reliably deleted (a legal or privacy request), and require retraining on every change; models also hallucinate neighbours of facts they were trained on. Retrieval gives citations, access control at query time, deletion by removing chunks, and updates by reindexing. Fine tuning is strong for format, style, domain phrasing, tool call syntax, and policies the model keeps forgetting. Hamel Husain (2024) summarises: fine tuning for syntax, style and rules; RAG for context and current facts. Combination: fine tune the generator to use retrieved context and cite in the required format, as the RAG paper's end to end training did.
say: I use retrieval for knowledge and fine tuning for behaviour. If the information changes, needs citations, or depends on who's asking, it belongs in an index, because I can update it, filter it per user and delete from it. Fine tuning shines for format, tone, and narrow skills, like always emitting a strict schema or using domain phrasing. Fine tuning facts in is the classic mistake: there are no citations, no deletion, a retrain for every doc change, and the model still confidently gets nearby facts wrong. They combine well, retrieval for what to say and fine tuning for how to say it.
must_mention: RAG for changing or cited facts
fine tuning for format, tone and skills
no citations or deletion with fine tuned facts

followups.q: Can fine tuning help a RAG system?
followups.a: Yes, fine tuning the generator to use retrieved passages and follow the citation format.

followups.q: What does fine tuning do badly?
followups.a: Injecting facts that change or must be traced, scoped per user or deleted.

traps: Proposing to fine tune the model on the documentation so it knows the docs.

topic: RAG versus fine tuning versus long context
q: What is the lost in the middle effect?
plain: Language models do not read a long prompt evenly. A 2023 study found they use information at the start and end of a long input much better than information in the middle. In one test with 20 retrieved documents, GPT-3.5-Turbo did worse when the answer sat in the middle than when it was given no documents at all. So stuffing more passages into a prompt can hurt, and where you put the best evidence matters.
deep: Liu et al. (2023), "Lost in the Middle": multi document QA and key value retrieval with controlled position of the relevant item. Accuracy follows a U shaped curve over position (primacy and recency bias). GPT-3.5-Turbo's closed book accuracy was 56.1 percent, and with the answer document in the middle of 20 or 30 documents it scored below that. Extended context versions (16K, 100K) performed about the same as their shorter counterparts when the input fit both. In open domain QA, reader accuracy saturated long before retriever recall: 50 instead of 20 documents added only about 1.5 points for GPT-3.5-Turbo and about 1 point for Claude 1.3. These are 2023 models; newer long context models do better on needle tests, so measure position sensitivity on your own data. Practical response: rerank, send fewer and better chunks, put the strongest evidence first.
say: It's the finding that models use information at the beginning and end of a long context much better than in the middle, a U shaped accuracy curve. In the 2023 paper, GPT 3.5 Turbo with the answer document buried in the middle of twenty documents actually scored below its closed book accuracy of about fifty six percent. They also found going from twenty to fifty retrieved documents barely helped. Newer models are better at this, so I don't treat the numbers as constants, but the lesson stands: more context isn't free, so I rerank, send fewer chunks, and put the best evidence first.
must_mention: middle placement below closed book in the 2023 study

followups.q: How would you test it on your system?
followups.a: Place a known answer passage at different positions among distractors and plot accuracy by position.

traps: Assuming a bigger context window means the model uses all of it equally.

topic: RAG versus fine tuning versus long context
q: When does putting everything in a long context window beat building a retrieval pipeline?
plain: When the whole knowledge base is small enough to fit in the prompt and you do not have many requests, sending all of it is simpler than building retrieval. Anthropic suggested a rough threshold of about 200,000 tokens, roughly 500 pages. Prompt caching makes it cheaper because the repeated part of the prompt is stored and reused. But you still pay for those tokens on every request, and models may miss facts in the middle. A 50 page employee handbook used by ten people a day is a good long context case; a million support tickets is not.
deep: Anthropic's contextual retrieval post (September 2024): under about 200k tokens, consider skipping RAG and loading the knowledge base into the prompt; prompt caching cuts latency by more than 2x and cost by up to 90 percent for the cached prefix. Against it: per request cost and latency scale with prompt length; position sensitivity (lost in the middle); citations and per user permissions are easier with chunk ids and retrieval filters; corpora grow. Decision procedure: run the same golden set through both designs and compare accuracy, citation precision, p95 latency and cost per query, then project with expected corpus growth and traffic.
say: When the corpus fits comfortably in the window, traffic is modest, and everyone can see everything. Anthropic's guidance was that under roughly two hundred thousand tokens, about five hundred pages, you can often skip retrieval and put the whole knowledge base in the prompt, with prompt caching cutting cost and latency a lot. I'd still check two things: whether the model actually finds facts placed in the middle, and what it costs per request at my traffic. If documents have per user permissions or the corpus will grow ten times, I'd build retrieval anyway.
must_mention: prompt caching reduces cost and latency

followups.q: What would you measure to decide?
followups.a: Accuracy, citation precision, p95 latency and cost per query for both designs on the same golden set.

traps: Ignoring per request token cost because caching exists.

topic: The RAG pipeline end to end
q: What happens offline, before any question arrives, in a RAG system?
plain: Before users ask anything, the system prepares its library. It collects documents, extracts clean text from PDFs and web pages, splits the text into chunks, labels each chunk with facts like source, date and who may see it, and stores the chunks in search indexes. A company wiki, for example, might become 200,000 labelled chunks stored once as vectors for meaning search and once as words for keyword search. Everything at question time depends on this preparation being right.
deep: Offline pipeline: fetch from source systems; parse (PDF layout, HTML boilerplate, XML structure, tables, OCR for scans); clean and deduplicate near copies; chunk; enrich with metadata (stable doc id, version, timestamp, page and section path, ACL and tenant, trust status such as retracted or superseded, language, doc type, optionally an LLM written contextual header); embed for dense retrieval and tokenise for an inverted (BM25) index; write both indexes. Metadata attached here drives filtering, freshness, deletion and citation later, so missing fields cannot be patched cheaply at query time. Index builds should be reproducible and versioned so an eval can name the index it ran against.
say: Offline is where the library gets built. I fetch documents from the source systems, parse them into clean text, which is harder than it sounds for PDFs and tables, deduplicate near copies, and split them into chunks. Each chunk gets metadata: a stable document id, version, date, section, who's allowed to see it, and any status like retracted or superseded. Then I embed the chunks into a vector index and also build a keyword index for BM25. Everything later, filtering, citations, deletion, depends on this metadata being there from the start.
must_mention: attach metadata including ACL and status

followups.q: Why deduplicate before indexing?
followups.a: Near copies fill the top k with the same content and waste the context budget.

traps: Treating ingestion as a one off script with no versioning.

topic: The RAG pipeline end to end
q: What happens online, from a user's question to the answer, in a RAG system?
plain: At question time the system first tidies the question, for example turning 'what about the annual one?' into a full query. It searches both indexes for maybe 100 candidate chunks, merges the lists, and uses a slower, more careful model to pick the best 5 to 20. The language model writes an answer from those chunks and cites them, and a final check confirms the citations support the claims or makes the system say it cannot answer. The key rule: the model can only use what retrieval handed it, so if the right chunk is missing, nothing later can fix it.
deep: Online pipeline: query rewriting with history, filter extraction, routing; hybrid retrieval of 100 to 150 candidates (dense plus BM25); fusion (RRF); cross encoder reranking to 5 to 20; prompt assembly with chunk ids, titles and dates within a token budget; generation with a citation per claim; post hoc verification of citations; an evidence gate deciding answer, hedge or refuse; trace logging (query, rewrites, ids and scores per stage, prompt and model versions, tokens, latency). Because recall at the context budget caps everything downstream, report stage metrics separately: recall at 100 for first stage, nDCG at 10 after reranking, faithfulness and citation precision for generation, false answer rate on unanswerables.
say: Online, I rewrite the question if it depends on chat history and pull out any filters like dates or product. Then I retrieve around a hundred candidates from both the vector and keyword indexes, fuse the lists, and rerank with a cross encoder down to maybe ten. The generator answers from those with citations, a verification step checks the citations actually support the claims, and if the evidence is weak the system says it can't answer. I log the whole trace. The rule I keep in mind is that retrieval recall caps the system, the model can't use what it never saw.

followups.q: Which stage would you measure first?
followups.a: Retrieval recall at the context budget, since downstream stages cannot recover a missing chunk.

traps: Describing only embed, search and generate.

topic: The RAG pipeline end to end
q: Where do RAG systems lose quality before retrieval even runs?
plain: In reading the documents. PDFs with two columns get read straight across both columns, tables become word soup when flattened, page headers repeat inside every chunk, and scanned pages have no text until OCR runs. If a price table is flattened into a jumble of numbers, no search engine or model can recover the price later. These failures are silent, so they need their own tests.
deep: Common parser failures: column order in multi column layouts; tables flattened row by row losing headers; repeated headers and footers polluting chunks; scanned pages needing OCR; HTML navigation and banners; structured XML edge cases (articles with no body, tables nested in paragraphs, deep section nesting, missing licence or permissions fields, non ASCII titles, related article references in unexpected formats). Near duplicate versions crowd the top k. Missing metadata breaks filters, freshness and deletion. Measure explicitly: parse error rate per source, manual spot checks of rendered chunks, and a golden set slice whose answers live in tables or figure captions. Keep a written log of parser failures found on real data; do not hide them by widening exception handling.
say: Mostly in parsing. Real PDFs have two column layouts read straight across, tables that turn into word soup, headers and footers repeated in every chunk, and scans with no text until OCR. If the parser mangles a table, no retriever or model downstream can recover the answer that was in it, and nothing errors, it just quietly gets worse. So I test parsing on its own: error rates per source, eyeballing rendered chunks, and a slice of test questions whose answers only exist in tables. And I keep a log of parser failures rather than swallowing them in a broad exception handler.

followups.q: How would you build a parsing test set?
followups.a: Pick documents per source and format, write questions answerable only from tables, figures or deep sections, and check the chunks contain the answer.

traps: Tuning embeddings when the text was never extracted correctly.

q: What is a chunk, and what is the trade off between small and large chunks?
plain: A chunk is the piece of a document that gets indexed, retrieved and cited as one unit, like an index card in a library. Small chunks describe one idea sharply, so a question about that idea finds them, but a chunk saying 'revenue grew 3 percent' without naming the company is useless on its own. Large chunks keep that context but mix several topics, so they match each topic weakly and use up more of the prompt. A 300 word chunk and a 2,000 word chunk of the same report will be retrieved for very different questions.
deep: Size sets precision of the embedding against completeness of context. A single vector for a long chunk averages several topics (mean pooling dilutes), so similarity to any one query drops; long chunks also consume the context budget, so fewer distinct hits fit. Short chunks give sharp vectors and precise citations but lose antecedents (the subject, the time period, the definitions). Mitigations combine both: retrieve small and return the parent section, or prepend contextual headers. DPR and the RAG paper used disjoint 100 word passages. The right size is an empirical question answered by recall at k on a golden set.
say: A chunk is the unit you embed, retrieve and cite. Its size trades precision against context. A small chunk embeds one idea cleanly, so it gets found for that idea, but it can lose its subject, like revenue grew three percent with no company or quarter. A large chunk keeps context, but its single vector averages several topics so it matches each one weakly, and it eats context budget, so fewer distinct hits fit in the prompt. I don't pick a size by intuition, I sweep sizes on a golden set and compare recall at the number of chunks I'll actually send.
must_mention: large: keeps context but dilutes the vector

followups.q: What chunk size did DPR and the RAG paper use?
followups.a: Disjoint 100 word passages from Wikipedia.

traps: Claiming there is one correct chunk size.

q: What chunking strategies do you know, and what does each trade off?
plain: You can cut text every few hundred tokens, at sentence or paragraph boundaries, along the document's own headings, or where the topic shifts. Fixed size is simple but cuts sentences and tables in half. Following headings keeps the author's own units, so a section titled 'Refund policy' stays together. Another option, parent child chunking, searches small pieces but hands the model the whole surrounding section. The right choice depends on the documents, and you test it rather than guess.
deep: Fixed token windows with overlap: predictable, but cut sentences, tables and code mid unit. Sentence or paragraph: coherent units, uneven sizes. Structure aware (headings, list items, functions in code): keeps author units and yields a section path for metadata, needs a parser per format. Semantic: split where similarity between adjacent sentence embeddings drops; topic coherent but an extra embedding pass and unstable boundaries. Parent child (small to big): embed small children for precise matching, return the parent section to the generator; two levels to store and sync. Late chunking and contextual headers restore document context to each chunk vector. Keep tables and code blocks whole whatever the strategy.
say: The main options are fixed token windows, usually with overlap, natural boundaries like sentences or paragraphs, structure aware splitting along headings or code functions, and semantic splitting where adjacent sentences stop being similar. Fixed windows are simple but cut sentences, tables and code in half. Structure aware keeps the author's units and gives me a section path for metadata. A useful hybrid is parent child: I match on small chunks for precision but hand the generator the whole parent section. Whatever the strategy, I keep tables and code blocks intact, and I choose by measured recall.

followups.q: What is the downside of semantic chunking?
followups.a: An extra embedding pass at index time and boundaries that shift when the model changes.

traps: Defaulting to fixed size windows without saying why.

q: How much does chunk overlap cost? Work an example.
plain: Overlap repeats the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so an answer sitting on a boundary appears whole in at least one chunk. The cost is more chunks to store and search. A 1,000 token document cut into 256 token chunks with 64 tokens of overlap gives 5 chunks; without overlap it gives 4. In general, 20 percent overlap makes the index about 1.25 times bigger, and 50 percent overlap doubles it.
deep:
With chunk size $s$ and overlap $o$, stride is $s - o$ and the count for a document of $L$ tokens is $1 + \lceil \max(0, L - s)/(s - o) \rceil$. For $L = 1000$, $s = 256$, $o = 64$: stride 192, $1 + \lceil 744/192 \rceil = 1 + 4 = 5$; with $o = 0$: $1 + \lceil 744/256 \rceil = 4$. With overlap share $r = o/s$, the number of chunks grows by about $1/(1-r)$: 1.11 at 10 percent, 1.25 at 20 percent, 2.0 at 50 percent (computed in Python). DPR reported that overlapping passages were not better than disjoint ones in its Wikipedia setting, so overlap is a choice to test, not a default.

```python
import math
def n_chunks(doc_tokens, size, overlap):
    return 1 + math.ceil(max(0, doc_tokens - size) / (size - overlap))
print(n_chunks(1000, 256, 64), n_chunks(1000, 256, 0))   # 5 4
```
say: Overlap means each chunk repeats the tail of the previous one, so an answer that straddles a boundary still appears whole somewhere. The cost is index size. With a thousand token document, two fifty six token chunks and sixty four tokens of overlap, the stride is one ninety two, so I get five chunks instead of four. As a rule, an overlap share of r grows the index by one over one minus r, so twenty percent overlap is about a quarter more chunks and fifty percent doubles it. DPR actually found overlap didn't help on Wikipedia, so I test it rather than assume it.
must_mention: test it, DPR found no gain

followups.q: What does overlap not fix?
followups.a: A chunk that lacks its subject because the subject was defined pages earlier; contextual headers or parent chunks fix that.

traps: Adding 50 percent overlap by default and doubling index cost.

q: What is late chunking?
plain: Normally each chunk is turned into a vector on its own, so it never sees the rest of its document. Late chunking first runs the whole document through the embedding model, then builds each chunk's vector from the word level outputs that fall inside that chunk. The chunk's vector therefore carries context from the rest of the document. For example, a chunk that says 'it grew 3 percent' can end up close to queries about the company named two paragraphs earlier.
deep: Standard: embed each chunk independently, so token representations attend only within the chunk. Late chunking: run a long context embedding model over the full document (or a large window), then mean pool the token embeddings within each chunk span to get chunk vectors; each token representation has attended to the whole document, so pronouns and implicit subjects are partly resolved. Requirements and costs: an encoder with a long enough window, one larger forward pass per document, and re embedding the whole document when any part changes. It targets the same failure as contextual retrieval (chunks losing their subject) without an LLM call per chunk. As with any chunking change, validate by recall at k on a golden set.
say: Late chunking flips the order. Instead of splitting first and embedding each chunk alone, I run the whole document through a long context embedding model, then pool the token level embeddings that fall inside each chunk's span. Every token has already attended to the full document, so a chunk that says it grew three percent carries some sense of what it refers to. It solves the same problem as contextual headers, chunks losing their subject, without an LLM call per chunk. The costs are needing an encoder with a long window and re embedding the whole document when part of it changes.
must_mention: pool token embeddings per chunk span

followups.q: When would you prefer contextual headers instead?
followups.a: When documents exceed the encoder window or you also want the added context in the BM25 index.

traps: Confusing late chunking with simply using bigger chunks.

q: What is contextual retrieval, and how much did it help?
plain: Contextual retrieval adds a short note to each chunk explaining where it comes from before the chunk is indexed. A model reads the whole document and the chunk and writes something like 'This is from ACME's Q2 2023 report, revenue section.' Anthropic reported that this cut missed retrievals from 5.7 percent of queries to 3.7 percent, and to 1.9 percent when combined with keyword search and reranking. It costs one model call per chunk when building the index.
deep: Anthropic (September 2024): Claude 3 Haiku receives the whole document and one chunk and writes 50 to 100 tokens situating the chunk, which is prepended before embedding (contextual embeddings) and before BM25 indexing (contextual BM25). Metric: 1 minus recall at 20, averaged across domains. Baseline 5.7 percent; contextual embeddings 3.7 percent (35 percent fewer failures); plus contextual BM25 2.9 percent (49 percent); plus reranking the top 150 to a top 20, 1.9 percent (67 percent). With prompt caching the one time cost was about USD 1.02 per million document tokens. Generic document summaries prepended to chunks helped little, so the context must be chunk specific. Maintenance: regenerate when documents change.
say: Contextual retrieval fixes chunks that lose their subject. Before indexing, a small model reads the whole document plus the chunk and writes a sentence or two placing it, like this is from Acme's second quarter report, revenue section, and that note is prepended for both embedding and the keyword index. Anthropic measured the share of queries missing a relevant chunk in the top twenty dropping from 5.7 percent to 3.7, then 2.9 with contextual BM25, then 1.9 with reranking. The cost is one cheap model call per chunk at index time, which prompt caching makes affordable.
must_mention: LLM written 50 to 100 token context per chunk

followups.q: What does it cost to maintain?
followups.a: Regenerating context whenever a document changes, plus slightly longer chunks to store.

traps: Thinking one generic document summary per chunk gives the same gain.

q: How would you choose the chunk size and strategy for a new corpus?
plain: Treat it as an experiment rather than a guess. Write a set of real questions and mark which passages answer them, then try a few chunk sizes and strategies and measure how often the right passage lands in the top results you would send to the model. Watch for practical traps, like the embedding model silently cutting off chunks longer than its limit. For example, you might find 300 token chunks split by headings find the answer in the top 5 for 82 percent of questions while 1,000 token windows manage 70 percent.
deep: Procedure: build a golden set of questions with gold passages (by document span, so it survives re chunking); sweep strategy (fixed, structure aware, semantic, parent child, contextual headers), size and overlap; for each config measure recall at the k you will feed the generator, plus downstream faithfulness on a sample; check token cost per query. Traps: embedding models truncate input beyond their max sequence length, so a 2,000 token chunk sent to a 512 token encoder is embedded from its first quarter; chunk level versus document level relevance (deduplicate chunks from the same document); tables and code must stay whole; fixed 512 token windows cut sentences at the edges. Choose the smallest configuration on the recall plateau.
say: I'd make it an experiment. First a golden set of real questions with the passages that answer them, marked by document span so the labels survive re chunking. Then I'd sweep a few strategies, fixed windows, heading based, parent child, maybe contextual headers, at a few sizes, and compare recall at the number of chunks I'd actually send, plus token cost. I'd check the embedding model's max length, because longer chunks get silently truncated, keep tables whole, and deduplicate chunks from the same document. Then I'd pick the cheapest setup on the recall plateau.
must_mention: recall at the k sent to the model

followups.q: What breaks at chunk edges with fixed 512 token windows?
followups.a: Sentences, tables and code cut mid unit, and references to a subject defined earlier.

traps: Choosing the chunk size by intuition or by a framework default.

q: What is an embedding, and what does a bi encoder do?
plain: An embedding is a list of numbers that places a piece of text on a map where texts with similar meaning sit close together. A bi encoder is a model that makes one such point for the question and, separately, one for every document. Because documents never need to see the question, all document points can be computed once, ahead of time. At question time you embed the question and look for the nearest stored points, so 'how do I get my money back' lands near a passage about refunds even though the words differ.
deep: A bi encoder (dual encoder) maps query and document independently: $s(q,d) = E_Q(q)^\top E_D(d)$ or cosine similarity. DPR used two BERT base encoders producing 768 dimensional vectors, with the CLS representation as the embedding. Document vectors are precomputed and indexed; query cost is one encoder forward pass plus a nearest neighbour search. Sentence vectors come from the CLS token or mean pooling over tokens; mean pooling over a long chunk averages topics, one reason large chunks retrieve worse. Some embedding models expect role prefixes such as "query:" and "passage:"; omitting them silently lowers recall, so follow the model card. Asymmetric retrieval (short questions, long passages) is the normal RAG case.
say: An embedding is a vector that places text in a space where similar meanings are close. A bi encoder embeds the query and each document independently, usually with a transformer, and scores relevance with a dot product or cosine. Because the document side never sees the query, I can embed the whole corpus offline and store the vectors in an index; a query then costs one encoder pass plus a nearest neighbour search. That's what makes dense retrieval fast enough for millions of documents. DPR is the textbook example, two BERT encoders producing seven hundred sixty eight dimensional vectors.
must_mention: vector where similar meanings are close

followups.q: What is pooling?
followups.a: Turning token vectors into one vector, by taking the CLS token or averaging tokens.

followups.q: Why do some models need a query or passage prefix?
followups.a: They were trained with those prefixes to handle asymmetric inputs; leaving them out lowers recall.

traps: Assuming any embedding model works the same for queries and passages.

q: Cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance: does the choice matter?
plain: For vectors scaled to length one, all three give exactly the same ranking, so the choice does not matter. If vectors are not normalised, the dot product also rewards long vectors, which some models use on purpose. The practical rule is to use the similarity the embedding model was trained with. For example, a model trained with cosine similarity should be searched with cosine, or with dot product after normalising the vectors.
deep: For unit vectors, $\lVert q - d \rVert^2 = \lVert q \rVert^2 + \lVert d \rVert^2 - 2\,q\cdot d = 2 - 2\,q \cdot d$, so ranking by smallest L2 distance equals ranking by largest dot product, which equals cosine. Without normalisation, $q \cdot d = \lVert q\rVert \lVert d\rVert \cos\theta$, so documents with large norms are favoured; some models encode a popularity or confidence signal in the norm. Indexes are often specified by metric (FAISS IndexFlatIP for inner product, normalise first for cosine). ColBERT normalises token embeddings so dot products are cosines in $[-1, 1]$.
say: If the vectors are normalised to unit length, it doesn't matter: squared Euclidean distance equals two minus two times the dot product, so all three give the same ranking. It matters when vectors aren't normalised, because then the dot product also rewards vector length, and some models are trained to put useful signal in the norm. So my rule is to match whatever the embedding model was trained with, and if it's cosine, normalise and use an inner product index. Mixing them up is a quiet way to lose recall.
must_mention: normalise for cosine with inner product index

followups.q: How do you get cosine search from an inner product index?
followups.a: L2 normalise all vectors, then inner product equals cosine.

traps: Using L2 distance on unnormalised vectors from a model trained with cosine.

q: What is a cross encoder, and how does it compare with a bi encoder?
plain: A cross encoder reads the question and one document together as a single input and outputs one relevance score, like a person laying the two side by side. That makes it much better at judging relevance, because it can compare individual words across the two. But nothing can be computed in advance, so it has to run once for every document you want to score. That is why bi encoders search the millions of documents and cross encoders only reorder the top hundred or so.
deep: Cross encoder: concatenate [query; document], full self attention across both, a classification or regression head gives one score. Cost: one forward pass per candidate over $|q| + |d|$ tokens, attention quadratic in that length, no precomputation. Bi encoder: independent encodings, precomputed document vectors, ANN search. Late interaction (ColBERT) sits between. BEIR (2021): BM25 top 100 reranked by a cross encoder averaged 11 percent above BM25 on nDCG at 10, best in the study, at about 450 ms per query on a V100 versus under 20 ms for dense retrieval on GPU. Standard design: bi encoder or hybrid for recall, cross encoder for precision on the shortlist.
say: A cross encoder concatenates the query with one document and runs full attention across both, then outputs a single relevance score. Because every query word can attend to every document word, it judges relevance much better than a bi encoder, which only compares two vectors made separately. The price is that nothing is precomputed, every candidate needs its own forward pass. So the standard design is a bi encoder, often with BM25, to pull a hundred candidates from millions, and a cross encoder to reorder those hundred. In BEIR that combination was the most accurate setup, at roughly twenty times the latency.
must_mention: too slow for the full corpus
retrieve with bi encoder, rerank with cross encoder

followups.q: Where does ColBERT fit?
followups.a: In between: per token vectors precomputed, scored by summed maximum similarity.

traps: Proposing a cross encoder for first stage retrieval over millions of documents.

q: Explain ColBERT's late interaction scoring and its main cost.
plain: ColBERT keeps one small vector for every word of a document instead of one vector for the whole thing. To score a question against a document, each question word finds its best matching document word, and those best match scores are added up. This keeps much of the word level detail a cross encoder sees, while document vectors are still computed ahead of time. The catch is size: storing a vector per word made one 15 million document index about 900 GB, against 18 GB for keyword search.
deep:
Khattab and Zaharia (SIGIR 2020). Shared BERT with [Q] and [D] marker tokens, linear projection to $m = 128$ dimensions, L2 normalisation; queries padded with mask tokens to $N_q = 32$ (query augmentation, essential in ablations); punctuation embeddings filtered from documents. Score:
$$S_{q,d} = \sum_{i \in |E_q|} \max_{j \in |E_d|} E_{q_i} \cdot E_{d_j}^\top$$
MaxSim is pruning friendly, so end to end retrieval uses a vector index over all token embeddings, then exact rescoring. As a reranker it ran over 170 times faster than BERT rerankers with about 14,000 times fewer FLOPs. Storage: BEIR reports about 900 GB for BioASQ (about 15M documents) versus 18 GB for BM25; zero shot it averaged 2.5 percent above BM25.
say: ColBERT is late interaction. It encodes query and document separately like a bi encoder, but keeps a hundred twenty eight dimensional vector for every token. The score is a sum over query tokens of each token's maximum similarity to any document token, MaxSim. That preserves word level matching, so quality gets close to a cross encoder, while the document side is still precomputed, and the paper reported over a hundred seventy times speedup over BERT reranking. The cost is storage, one vector per token, which made a fifteen million document index about nine hundred gigabytes in BEIR versus eighteen for BM25.
must_mention: sum over query tokens of max similarity

followups.q: Why pad queries with mask tokens?
followups.a: Query augmentation lets the model produce extra query embeddings that act like soft expansion terms; ablations showed it matters.

traps: Calling ColBERT a cross encoder.

q: What kinds of queries do dense embeddings handle badly?
plain: Embeddings capture general meaning but blur exact details. Product codes, order numbers, error messages, rare names, specific figures and words like 'not' are often lost when a whole passage is squeezed into one vector. A search for error 'E1043' may return passages about other errors that sound similar. That is the main reason good systems pair embeddings with keyword search.
deep: A single dense vector is a lossy bottleneck trained to capture topical similarity. Weak spots: exact identifiers (SKUs, error codes, ticket ids), numbers and units, rare entities and new terminology absent from training data, negation and contrast ("does not support" versus "supports"), and long passages whose vector averages topics. Lexical retrieval (BM25) is exact on these, which is why hybrid search with rank fusion is the default in production. Diagnose by slicing the golden set: identifier queries, numeric queries, negation queries, and compare dense, BM25 and hybrid recall per slice.
say: Dense embeddings capture topic and paraphrase well but blur exact details. Product codes, error strings, ticket numbers, rare names, specific numbers, and negation all tend to get lost when a whole passage is compressed into one vector, so a query for one error code can come back with passages about similar sounding errors. BM25 is exact on those tokens, which is the main reason I run hybrid search. To check, I slice the golden set by query type, identifiers, numbers, negations, and compare dense, keyword and hybrid recall on each slice.

followups.q: How would you show the problem to a team?
followups.a: Recall by query slice: identifier and numeric queries where BM25 beats dense.

traps: Assuming a stronger embedding model fixes exact match queries.

q: What did the BEIR benchmark show about dense retrievers on new domains?
plain: BEIR tested retrieval models on 18 datasets they were not trained on, from biomedical papers to tweets. A well known dense retriever trained on Google style questions scored about 48 percent worse than plain keyword search on average, while keyword search followed by a cross encoder reranker scored 11 percent better. Models that do well on their training data do not automatically do well elsewhere. So you test on your own domain before trusting a leaderboard.
deep: Thakur et al. (2021): 18 datasets, 9 task types, zero shot, nDCG at 10. Average relative to BM25: DPR minus 47.7 percent, ANCE minus 7.4, TAS-B minus 2.8, GenQ minus 3.6, DeepCT minus 27.9, SPARTA minus 20.3, docT5query plus 1.6, ColBERT plus 2.5, BM25 plus cross encoder plus 11. In domain performance correlated poorly with out of domain generalisation. Efficiency: dense retrieval about 14 to 20 ms on GPU with 3 GB index per 1M docs; BM25 20 ms on CPU, 0.4 GB. A measurement caveat: many datasets were annotated from lexically pooled candidates, biasing judgments toward BM25. Fixes: hybrid search, domain adaptation (GenQ helped on specialised domains), rerankers.
say: BEIR evaluated retrievers zero shot on eighteen datasets across nine task types, scored by nDCG at ten. The headline was that BM25 was a strong baseline: DPR, trained on Natural Questions, came out about forty eight percent below BM25 on average, the better dense models were still a few percent below, and BM25 plus a cross encoder reranker was about eleven percent above. In domain wins didn't predict out of domain performance. There's a caveat that many datasets were labelled from keyword search candidates, which favours BM25, but the practical lesson holds: evaluate on your own domain and keep BM25 in the mix.

followups.q: Why might the benchmark favour BM25?
followups.a: Relevance labels were often collected from BM25 style candidate pools, so documents only dense models find were never judged.

traps: Picking an embedding model by its MS MARCO score alone.

q: How is a dense retriever trained? Write the contrastive loss.
plain: You train it like a matching game. For each question you show the model the correct passage and several wrong ones, and the loss punishes it unless the correct passage gets the highest score. Technically it is a softmax over the candidates with the correct passage as the label. For example, if a question about refunds scores 0.9 with the refund passage but 0.95 with a shipping passage, the loss is high and training pulls the refund passage closer.
deep:
DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020), for query $q_i$, positive $p_i^+$, negatives $p_{i,j}^-$:
$$L = -\log \frac{e^{\mathrm{sim}(q_i,p_i^+)}}{e^{\mathrm{sim}(q_i,p_i^+)} + \sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{\mathrm{sim}(q_i,p_{i,j}^-)}}$$
This is softmax cross entropy with the positive as the target class (the InfoNCE family). With a temperature $\tau$, similarities are divided by $\tau$ first; small $\tau$ sharpens the softmax and concentrates gradient on the hardest negatives. The gradient raises the positive's similarity and lowers each negative's in proportion to its softmax probability. DPR's full retriever beat Lucene BM25 by 9 to 19 points of top 20 retrieval accuracy across open domain QA datasets.
say: It's contrastive. For each query I have one positive passage and a set of negatives, and the loss is the negative log of the softmax probability of the positive among all of them, so it's cross entropy where the right passage is the label. Gradients push the query toward its positive and away from each negative in proportion to how much probability that negative was stealing. A temperature divides the similarities first, and a small temperature focuses learning on the hardest negatives. DPR trained this way beat BM25 by nine to nineteen points of top twenty accuracy on open domain QA.
must_mention: cross entropy with positive as label
DPR beat BM25 on its datasets

followups.q: What does the gradient do to a negative with high similarity?
followups.a: Pushes it away strongly, since its share of the softmax probability is large.

traps: Writing a pointwise binary loss and calling it contrastive retrieval training.

q: What are in batch negatives, and why do bigger batches help?
plain: In a batch of question and passage pairs, every other question's correct passage can serve as a wrong option for this question, for free. With a batch of 128 pairs, each question gets 127 negatives without fetching anything extra. More negatives make the training task closer to the real job of picking one passage from a whole collection. In the DPR paper, accuracy kept rising as the batch grew.
deep: Embed $B$ pairs into $Q, P \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d}$; compute $S = QP^\top$ ($B \times B$); apply cross entropy row wise with targets on the diagonal. Each query gets $B-1$ negatives and one batch covers $B^2$ query passage pairs, reusing computation. They are better than random negatives because they are other real positives, plausible text on real topics. DPR (Natural Questions dev, top 20 accuracy): 69.1, 70.8, 73.0 with 7, 31 and 127 in batch negatives. Hence large batches, gradient caching, or memory banks of past embeddings. Pitfall: duplicates in a batch (two queries sharing a gold passage) create false negatives, so deduplicate.
say: In batch negatives reuse the other examples in the batch. I embed B queries and their B positive passages, take the B by B matrix of all query passage dot products, and treat the diagonal as the correct answers, so each query gets the other B minus one passages as negatives for free. They're more useful than random passages because they're real positives for other queries, so they're on topic for something. Bigger batches mean more negatives and a task closer to ranking the whole corpus, and DPR's top twenty accuracy rose steadily as in batch negatives went from seven to a hundred twenty seven.
must_mention: other positives in the batch as negatives

followups.q: What can go wrong?
followups.a: Duplicate passages in a batch become false negatives; deduplicate when building batches.

traps: Calling in batch negatives random negatives.

q: Implement an in batch InfoNCE loss in numpy.
plain: The code normalises the question and passage vectors, builds the table of all question to passage similarities, divides by a temperature, and takes a cross entropy where the correct passage for each question sits on the diagonal. With correctly paired passages the loss is near zero; shuffle the pairing and it jumps. Raising the temperature from 0.05 to 1.0 makes the same correct pairing look uncertain, because the scores are no longer spread apart. Running it is a quick sanity check on any retriever training loop.
deep:
```python
import numpy as np

def info_nce(q, p, temperature=0.05):
    q = q / np.linalg.norm(q, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    p = p / np.linalg.norm(p, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    logits = q @ p.T / temperature                 # B x B
    logits -= logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)    # stability
    log_probs = logits - np.log(np.exp(logits).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return -np.mean(np.diag(log_probs))            # targets on the diagonal

q = np.array([[1.0, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0], [0.7, 0.7]])
p = np.array([[0.9, 0.2], [0.1, 0.9], [0.6, 0.8]])
print(round(info_nce(q, p), 4), round(info_nce(q, p[[1, 2, 0]]), 4), round(info_nce(q, p, 1.0), 4))
# 0.0296 7.5251 0.8638
```
Aligned pairs give 0.0296, misaligned 7.5251, and temperature 1.0 gives 0.8638, near the chance value $\ln 3 \approx 1.10$, because cosines in $[0, 1]$ barely separate without scaling. Subtracting the row max before exponentiating avoids overflow.
say: I L2 normalise queries and passages, compute the B by B matrix of dot products divided by a temperature, subtract each row's max for numerical stability, take a log softmax across each row, and average the negative log probability on the diagonal, since the diagonal holds each query's true passage. On a toy batch of three, correctly aligned pairs gave a loss of about 0.03 and shuffled pairs about 7.5. With temperature one instead of 0.05 the aligned loss was 0.86, close to log three, because cosine similarities between zero and one barely separate unless you scale them.

followups.q: Why make the loss symmetric?
followups.a: Adding the column wise loss (passage to query) uses the same matrix and often helps; it is a common variant.

traps: Forgetting the stability shift and overflowing exp at low temperature.

q: What are hard negatives, and how much did they help DPR?
plain: A hard negative is a wrong passage that looks right: it shares the question's words but does not contain the answer. Random wrong passages are too easy to tell apart, so the model learns little from them. Hard negatives force it to learn finer distinctions. In the DPR paper, adding just one keyword search hard negative per question raised the share of questions with the answer in the top 5 from 55.8 to 65.8 percent.
deep: DPR ablation (Natural Questions dev, top k accuracy): in batch training with 127 gold negatives reached 55.8 top 5 and 73.0 top 20; adding one BM25 negative per question (top BM25 passage not containing the answer, shared across the batch) gave 65.8 top 5 and 78.0 top 20. A second BM25 negative did not help further. Sources of hard negatives: BM25 top hits without the answer, the current dense model's top hits (refreshed during training, as in ANCE style mining), or cross encoder ranked candidates. Their value is the gradient signal near the decision boundary.
say: A hard negative is a passage that the current system would rank highly, it shares the query's words or topic, but it doesn't actually answer the question. Random negatives are trivially separable, so the gradient from them is almost zero, while hard negatives teach the fine distinctions that matter at the top of the ranking. DPR showed it cleanly: with in batch negatives alone, top five accuracy on Natural Questions was about fifty six percent, and adding a single BM25 hard negative per question pushed it to about sixty six. A second one didn't add more.
must_mention: looks relevant but lacks the answer
mine from BM25 or the current model

followups.q: Where else can hard negatives come from?
followups.a: The dense model's own top hits, refreshed as it trains, or candidates ranked by a cross encoder.

traps: Using only random negatives and expecting good top k ranking.

q: Why can hard negative mining hurt, and how do you prevent it?
plain: Relevance labels are sparse, so many of the 'wrong' passages the system scores highest are actually correct, just never labelled. Training on them teaches the model to push good answers away. You catch this by checking the top mined negatives by hand, filtering them with a stronger model, and watching held out recall rather than training loss. For example, a question about 'refund window' may have three valid passages but only one labelled, and the other two become poisonous negatives.
deep: False negatives: unlabelled positives among mined hard negatives, and duplicates in batch. Effects: training loss improves while dev recall stalls or falls. Mitigations: score mined candidates with a cross encoder and drop those above a relevance threshold; sample negatives from a rank band below the very top (skip the top few); deduplicate passages within batches; distil from a cross encoder teacher so soft scores replace hard labels (margin based losses); refresh negatives with the current model; manually audit samples. Validate with a labelled dev set that includes multiple positives per query where possible.
say: The danger is false negatives. Labels in retrieval are sparse, so when I mine the highest scoring passages that aren't marked positive, a good share are actually relevant, just unlabelled, and training pushes them away. The symptom is training loss improving while dev recall stalls or drops. I handle it by scoring mined negatives with a cross encoder and dropping anything it rates likely relevant, sampling negatives from a band below the very top, deduplicating passages within each batch, and spot checking them by hand. Distilling from a cross encoder's soft scores sidesteps hard labels altogether.

followups.q: Why refresh negatives during training?
followups.a: As the model improves, old hard negatives become easy, so mining with the current model keeps them informative.

traps: Assuming every unlabelled passage is irrelevant.

q: How do you adapt a dense retriever to a new domain with no labelled queries?
plain: Generate the training data. A language model reads passages from the new domain and writes questions each passage answers, and you fine tune the retriever on those made up pairs. BEIR's version of this, called GenQ, helped on specialised areas like scientific papers and finance but slightly hurt on general Wikipedia text. Another route is to train the fast retriever to imitate a slower, stronger reranker's scores.
deep: Synthetic query generation: for each passage, an LLM (or a T5 query generator) writes plausible queries; train the bi encoder contrastively on (synthetic query, passage) pairs with in batch and mined negatives. BEIR's GenQ fine tuned TAS-B this way: better on specialised domains (scientific, financial, StackExchange), weaker on broad Wikipedia style domains. Distillation: score candidate pairs with a cross encoder teacher and train the bi encoder to match its scores or margins, transferring quality to the cheap architecture. Validate on a small hand labelled set from the target domain; synthetic queries can be too easy (lexically copied from the passage) or off distribution compared with real user questions.
say: Without labels I'd generate them. An LLM reads passages from the new domain and writes questions each passage answers, and I fine tune the bi encoder contrastively on those synthetic pairs. BEIR's GenQ did exactly that on top of TAS B and it helped on specialised domains like scientific papers and finance, though it slightly hurt on general Wikipedia. The other route is distillation, scoring candidates with a cross encoder and training the bi encoder to match its scores. Either way I'd hand label a small target domain set to validate, because synthetic questions tend to copy words from the passage and come out too easy.
must_mention: validate on a small labelled set

followups.q: What is the risk of synthetic queries?
followups.a: They copy wording from the passage, so they are easier and more lexical than real questions.

traps: Trusting synthetic query metrics as if they were real user metrics.

topic: Vector indexes: flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ
q: What is exact (flat) vector search, and when is it enough?
plain: Flat search compares the question's vector with every stored vector and returns the closest ones. It is always exact, so it is the gold standard other methods are measured against. Its cost grows in direct proportion to the number of vectors, and memory is the full vectors: 10 million vectors of 768 numbers take about 30.7 GB. For a few hundred thousand vectors it is fast enough and needs no tuning at all.
deep: Cost per query $O(Nd)$ multiply adds; memory $4d$ bytes per float32 vector (FAISS IndexFlatL2 or IndexFlatIP), so $10^7 \times 768 \times 4 = 30.72$ GB (15.36 GB in float16). Exact search is the right choice for small corpora (up to roughly hundreds of thousands to a million vectors, depending on latency budget and hardware, GPUs make it fast), for small filtered subsets, and always as ground truth when measuring ANN recall. It supports exact deletes simply. Beyond that, approximate indexes trade recall for speed and memory.
say: Flat search computes the similarity between the query and every stored vector and returns the true top k. It's exact, needs no training or tuning, and deletes are trivial, so for a few hundred thousand vectors, or a small filtered subset, it's often the right answer. The cost is linear in the number of vectors, and memory is the raw vectors, so ten million seven hundred sixty eight dimensional float32 vectors are about thirty one gigabytes. I also always keep flat search around as ground truth, because approximate indexes are measured by how much of the exact top k they recover.

followups.q: How much memory for 10M by 768 float16?
followups.a: About 15.4 GB.

traps: Reaching for an ANN index for a corpus of 50,000 chunks.

topic: Vector indexes: flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ
q: What does recall mean for an approximate nearest neighbour index, and how is it different from retrieval recall?
plain: For an ANN index, recall means: of the true nearest vectors that exact search would return, what share did the fast index find. It says nothing about whether those vectors are relevant to the question. Retrieval recall, by contrast, asks whether the relevant documents were found. A perfect ANN index over a poor embedding model will faithfully return the wrong passages; for example, 99 percent ANN recall can coexist with 40 percent retrieval recall.
deep: ANN recall at k $= |\text{ANN top}k \cap \text{exact top}k| / k$, computed against flat search over the same vectors (the HNSW paper defines recall as found true nearest neighbours over K). Retrieval recall at k $= |\text{relevant} \cap \text{top}k| / R$ against human qrels. The two are often conflated in interviews and vendor benchmarks. ANN recall bounds how much of the embedding model's quality you keep; past about 0.95 it usually moves downstream nDCG little, while the embedding model, chunking and hybrid search move it a lot. Report both, and tune ANN at a target recall.
say: ANN recall measures how faithfully the index approximates exact search: of the true top k nearest vectors, what fraction did it return. Retrieval recall measures relevance: of the documents that actually answer the question, what fraction made the top k. They're different things, and mixing them up is a common interview trap. An index can have ninety nine percent ANN recall over a weak embedding model and still retrieve the wrong passages. So I tune the index to a target ANN recall against flat search, and separately measure retrieval recall against labelled queries.
must_mention: share of exact top k found

followups.q: Does pushing ANN recall from 0.95 to 0.99 matter?
followups.a: Usually little for end to end quality, at a real latency cost; measure downstream nDCG to decide.

traps: Reporting ANN recall as if it measured answer quality.

q: How does an IVF index work, and what does nprobe control?
plain: IVF groups the stored vectors into neighbourhoods using k-means clustering. At question time it finds the few neighbourhood centres closest to the question and only searches the vectors in those neighbourhoods, which nprobe sets. Searching more neighbourhoods finds more true neighbours but takes longer. In a small test with 64 neighbourhoods, searching 1 found 30 percent of the true top 10 and searching 16 found 87 percent, while still skipping three quarters of the data.
deep: Train k-means with nlist centroids; each vector goes into the inverted list of its nearest centroid. Query: rank centroids by distance, scan the nprobe nearest lists exhaustively. Work about $nlist \cdot d + (nprobe/nlist)\,N d$. Recall is lost when a true neighbour lies in an unprobed cell, mostly for queries near cell boundaries. FAISS rule of thumb: $nlist \approx C\sqrt{N}$ (for $N = 10^7$ and $C = 4$, about 12,649). Bytes per vector for IVF Flat: $4d + 8$ (an 8 byte id). Toy run (20,000 vectors, 32 dimensions, overlapping clusters, nlist 64): recall at 10 of 0.297, 0.409, 0.550, 0.709, 0.865 at nprobe 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, scanning 1.6 to 24 percent of vectors; with well separated clusters nprobe 2 already gave 0.994. Distribution drift after training unbalances cells.
say: IVF, an inverted file index, runs k-means over the vectors to get some number of centroids, nlist, and files each vector under its nearest centroid. At query time it ranks the centroids by distance to the query and only scans the vectors in the nprobe closest cells. So nprobe is the recall versus latency knob: probe more cells, find more true neighbours, scan more data. In a toy test with sixty four cells, one probe found thirty percent of the true top ten and sixteen probes found eighty seven percent. How clustered your embeddings are decides how many probes you need.
must_mention: nlist about C times square root of N

followups.q: Why might IVF degrade over time?
followups.a: If new data drifts from the training distribution, cells become unbalanced; retrain the centroids.

traps: Using IVF without ever measuring recall at the chosen nprobe.

topic: Vector indexes: flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ
q: What is product quantization, and why is it used?
plain: Product quantization shrinks each vector so far more fit in memory. It cuts the vector into small pieces and replaces each piece with the number of its closest entry in a learned list of 256 typical pieces, which fits in one byte. A 768 number vector that took 3,072 bytes becomes 96 bytes, about 32 times smaller. Distances become approximate, so systems often double check the best candidates with the full vectors.
deep: Split $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ into $M$ subvectors of $d/M$ dimensions; learn a k-means codebook of $2^{nbits}$ centroids per subspace (256 for 8 bits); store the $M$ centroid ids. Code size $\lceil M \cdot nbits / 8 \rceil$ bytes (FAISS IndexPQ), plus 8 bytes per id in IVF PQ. Asymmetric distance: precompute a table of query subvector to centroid distances per subspace, then a code's distance is a sum of $M$ table lookups, so scanning is fast. Lossy: quantization error reorders close candidates, so rerank a shortlist with full precision vectors. FAISS calls IVF PQ the most common choice for large scale search. Alternatives: scalar quantization to 8 bits ($d$ bytes), lower dimensional embeddings.
say: Product quantization compresses vectors. I split each vector into M subvectors, learn a codebook of two hundred fifty six centroids for each subspace with k-means, and store just the one byte id of the nearest centroid per subvector. So a seven hundred sixty eight dimensional float vector, about three thousand bytes, becomes ninety six bytes with M of ninety six. Distances are computed with lookup tables of query to centroid distances, which makes scanning fast. It's lossy, so I usually rerank the shortlist with full precision vectors. Combined with IVF, it's the standard for very large indexes.

followups.q: Why not just use fewer dimensions?
followups.a: That also works and can combine with PQ; it changes the embedding itself, while PQ approximates a fixed embedding.

traps: Treating PQ distances as exact.

q: How does HNSW search work at a high level?
plain: HNSW builds a layered map of the vectors, like a road network with motorways on top and side streets at the bottom. Only a few points are on the top layer, linked by long jumps; every point is on the bottom layer, linked to its close neighbours. A search starts at the top, keeps hopping to whichever linked point is closer to the question, then drops a layer and repeats. It gives very good accuracy at low latency, but it keeps all vectors in memory and does not handle deletions well.
deep: Malkov and Yashunin: a hierarchy of proximity graphs, a skip list generalised to graphs. Element levels decay exponentially, so upper layers are sparse with long range links. Search: from the entry point on the top layer, greedily move to the neighbour closest to the query until no neighbour is closer (a local minimum), descend and restart from there; on layer 0 keep a dynamic candidate list of size efSearch with backtracking, return the best k. Complexity scales as $O(\log N)$. Strong speed recall trade off; memory is raw vectors plus graph links; FAISS's IndexHNSW does not support removing vectors.
say: HNSW is a layered proximity graph, basically a skip list built out of graphs. Every vector is in the bottom layer with links to near neighbours, and a random, exponentially shrinking subset is also in higher layers with longer range links. A search starts at an entry point on the top layer, greedily hops to whichever neighbour is closer to the query until it can't improve, drops down a layer and continues, and on the bottom layer it keeps a small beam of candidates. Search cost grows roughly with the log of the dataset size, which is why it's fast, but it holds everything in RAM and deletes are awkward.
must_mention: sparse top layers with long links
logarithmic scaling, memory heavy, poor deletes

followups.q: Why is it called navigable small world?
followups.a: The graphs let greedy routing reach any target in few hops, like small world social networks.

traps: Saying HNSW is exact search.

topic: Vector indexes: flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ
q: What do HNSW's M, efConstruction and efSearch parameters control?
plain: M is how many links each point gets in the graph: more links find neighbours more reliably but cost memory. efConstruction is how hard the builder searches when adding each point: higher builds a better graph more slowly. efSearch is how many candidates the search keeps open: higher finds more true neighbours but each query takes longer. For example, raising efSearch from 16 to 128 typically buys recall at the price of several times the latency, so you tune it to a recall target.
deep: M: links per node on upper layers; layer 0 allows $M_{max0} = 2M$ (paper's recommendation; higher degrades performance and wastes memory). Reasonable M is about 5 to 48: small M for low recall or low dimensional data, larger M for high recall and high dimensional data; graph memory is proportional to M. efConstruction: candidate list size during insertion; must be large enough that construction recall is near 1 (0.95 is enough for most cases per the paper); the paper built a 10M SIFT index with efConstruction 100 in about 3 minutes on a 40 core server. efSearch: candidate list size on layer 0 at query time, at least k; the main online recall versus latency knob. Tune efSearch per target recall measured against flat search.
say: M is the number of neighbours each node links to, doubled on the bottom layer, and it sets memory and the ceiling on recall; the paper suggests somewhere around five to forty eight, larger for high dimensional data and high recall. ef construction is the candidate list size used while inserting, so it trades build time for graph quality. ef search is the candidate list size at query time, at least k, and it's the knob I actually tune in production: raise it until I hit the recall target against exact search, then read off latency. M and ef construction are fixed once the index is built.
must_mention: M links per node, 2M on layer 0
M sets memory and recall ceiling
tune efSearch to a recall target

followups.q: Which parameters can change without rebuilding?
followups.a: efSearch; M and efConstruction are fixed at build time.

traps: Tuning efSearch without measuring recall against exact search.
