q: How does HNSW assign layers and choose neighbours, and how much memory does the graph take?
plain: Each new point rolls a random number that decides its top layer, with each higher layer about M times less likely, so upper layers stay sparse. When linking a point, HNSW does not just take its closest neighbours; it skips a candidate that is already closer to a chosen neighbour than to the new point, which keeps links pointing in different directions and keeps clusters connected. The graph itself costs roughly 60 to 450 bytes per vector for typical settings, about 151 bytes at M equal to 16.
deep: Level: $l = \lfloor -\ln(U)\, m_L \rfloor$, $U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, with $m_L = 1/\ln M$, equivalent to a skip list with $p = 1/M$ and about one element of overlap between layers; the expected maximum level grows as $O(\log N)$, giving $O(\log N)$ search. Neighbour heuristic (Algorithm 4): consider candidates by distance and add one only if it is closer to the inserted element than to every already selected neighbour; this approximates the relative neighbourhood graph and preserves edges between clusters (Fig. 2 of the paper). Memory: $(M_{max0} + m_L M_{max}) \cdot 4$ bytes per element with 4 byte ids; with $M_{max0} = 2M$: 61 bytes at M = 6, 151 at M = 16, 434 at M = 48 (computed), matching the paper's 60 to 450 byte range. Raw vectors are stored in addition.
say: Levels are drawn as the floor of minus log of a uniform random number times m L, with m L equal to one over log M, so each layer up is about M times sparser, like a skip list, and the number of layers grows with log N. For neighbours, the heuristic walks candidates in distance order and keeps one only if it's closer to the new node than to any neighbour already kept, which spreads links in different directions and keeps separate clusters connected. Graph memory is about M max zero plus m L times M max, times four bytes, so roughly a hundred fifty bytes per vector at M of sixteen, on top of the vectors.
must_mention: level equals floor of minus ln U times mL
memory about (2M plus M over ln M) times 4 bytes

followups.q: What happens if mL is zero?
followups.a: Everything is on one layer, giving a flat k-NN graph with much worse, power law search scaling.

traps: Thinking HNSW simply links each node to its M nearest neighbours.

topic: Vector indexes: flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ
q: You need to serve 100 million 768 dimensional embeddings. How do you size and choose the index?
plain: Start with arithmetic: 100 million vectors of 768 four byte numbers is about 307 GB, more than one machine's memory. HNSW keeps those vectors plus about 150 bytes of links each, so it would need several machines. Compressing with IVF plus product quantization stores about 104 bytes per vector, roughly 10 GB, at some cost in accuracy that you win back by rescoring the top few hundred with full vectors. Then you pick settings by measured recall, not defaults.
deep: Raw float32: $10^8 \times 768 \times 4 = 307$ GB (float16: 154 GB). HNSW at M = 16: plus about 151 bytes per vector of links, about 322 GB total: shard across machines. IVF PQ with $M = 96$ one byte codes plus 8 byte ids: $10^8 \times 104 = 10.4$ GB; nlist about $4\sqrt{N} = 40{,}000$; tune nprobe to target recall; rerank the top few hundred with full precision vectors held on disk or a separate tier. Middle options: scalar quantization to 8 bits (768 bytes per vector, 77 GB), smaller embedding dimensions, sharded HNSW. Decide at matched recall on a sampled query set with flat search ground truth, then compare p99 latency, memory and update cost (deletes, re embedding).
say: First the arithmetic: a hundred million times seven sixty eight floats at four bytes is about three hundred gigabytes, so exact vectors in RAM already means sharding, and HNSW adds roughly a hundred fifty bytes of links per vector on top. If memory is the constraint, I'd use IVF with product quantization: ninety six one byte codes plus an id is about a hundred bytes a vector, around ten gigabytes total. PQ costs accuracy, so I'd rerank the top few hundred with full precision vectors. Then I'd tune nprobe on a sample to hit a recall target against exact search and compare latency at that point.
must_mention: HNSW adds about 151 bytes per vector

followups.q: How would deletes work?
followups.a: IVF lists can remove ids; for HNSW use tombstones and periodic rebuilds.

traps: Forgetting that HNSW keeps the raw vectors in memory as well as the graph.

topic: Vector indexes: flat, IVF, HNSW, PQ
q: How would you benchmark two vector indexes fairly?
plain: Compare them at the same accuracy rather than at their default settings, because defaults sit at different points on the speed versus accuracy curve. Pick a target such as finding 95 percent of the true top 10, tune each index until it hits that target on your own queries, then compare speed, memory and build time. Include queries with filters, which some indexes handle badly. Finally check that the gain matters for answer quality, not just for raw search.
deep: Procedure: sample real queries; compute ground truth with flat search on the same vectors; sweep knobs (nprobe; efSearch; M; PQ size) to trace recall versus latency curves; compare at matched recall (for example 0.95 at k = 10) on p50 and p99 latency, QPS, memory, build time and update and delete cost; repeat for filtered queries. Data distribution matters: in my toy IVF, overlapping clusters needed nprobe 16 for 0.865 recall while well separated clusters reached 0.994 at nprobe 2. Then check end to end retrieval metrics against qrels, since gains in ANN recall past about 0.95 often barely move nDCG, while embedding choice moves it a lot.
say: I'd compare at matched recall. Each index's defaults sit at a different point on its recall versus latency curve, so comparing defaults says nothing. I'd take real queries, compute exact neighbours with flat search, sweep each index's knobs to trace its curve, and read off p50 and p99 latency, memory and build time at, say, ninety five percent recall at ten. I'd rerun with filters, because some indexes degrade badly there. And I'd check end to end relevance, because past a point extra ANN recall barely moves nDCG, while the embedding model moves it a lot.
must_mention: p99 latency, memory, build and update cost
filtered queries and end to end relevance

followups.q: Why does data distribution matter?
followups.a: Clustered embeddings let IVF find neighbours in few cells; diffuse ones need many more probes.

traps: Reporting queries per second without the recall it was measured at.

q: What is sparse retrieval, and what is an inverted index?
plain: Sparse retrieval represents text by the words it contains, and almost all possible words are absent from any one document, hence 'sparse'. An inverted index is like the index at the back of a book: for every word it lists the documents that contain it. To answer a query, the engine looks up each query word's list and scores only the documents that appear in them. A query for 'refund policy' touches only documents containing 'refund' or 'policy', which is why keyword search is so fast.
deep: Each document is a bag of terms, a vector over the vocabulary that is mostly zeros. The inverted index maps term to a postings list of (document id, term frequency, often positions). Query evaluation scores only documents in the union of the query terms' postings, using a scoring function such as TF IDF or BM25; dynamic pruning algorithms skip low scoring documents. Index size is small (BEIR: 0.4 GB for 1M DBPedia documents) and latency low (20 ms on CPU). Analysis choices (tokenisation, lowercasing, stemming, stop words) change results and belong in the evaluated configuration. Learned sparse models (DeepCT, SPARTA, document expansion like docT5query) keep the inverted index but learn the term weights or added terms.
say: Sparse retrieval represents documents as bags of words, vectors over the whole vocabulary that are almost entirely zeros. An inverted index stores, for each term, the list of documents that contain it, with term counts. To answer a query you only touch the postings lists of the query terms and score those documents, which is why keyword search is fast and cheap: BEIR measured about twenty milliseconds per query on CPU over a million documents with a small index. Choices like tokenisation and stemming change what matches, so they're part of the configuration I evaluate.

followups.q: What is document expansion?
followups.a: Adding generated queries or terms to documents before indexing, as docT5query does, to reduce vocabulary mismatch.

traps: Thinking keyword search needs a vector database.

q: Write the BM25 scoring formula.
plain: BM25 adds up a score for each word in the query. Each word's score is its rarity across the collection times how often it appears in the document, with two adjustments: extra repeats count less and less, and long documents are marked down because they contain more words by chance. Rare words like 'chargeback' count far more than common ones like 'account'. It is the default ranking function in most search engines.
deep:
Robertson and Zaragoza (2009):
$$\mathrm{BM25}(D,Q) = \sum_{t\in Q} \mathrm{IDF}(t)\,\frac{f(t,D)\,(k_1+1)}{f(t,D) + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|D|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)}$$
with $f(t,D)$ the count of $t$ in $D$, $|D|$ the document length, avgdl the mean length. The common Lucene IDF is $\ln\left(\frac{N - n(t) + 0.5}{n(t) + 0.5} + 1\right)$ with $N$ documents and $n(t)$ containing $t$; the "+1" keeps it positive, whereas the original Robertson Sparck Jones form goes negative for terms in more than half the documents. Typical $k_1 \in [1.2, 2.0]$, $b = 0.75$. Variants: BM25F weights fields, BM25+ adds a lower bound $\delta$ so long documents are not over penalised.
say: BM25 sums over query terms. Each term contributes its IDF, which is roughly the log of how rare the term is across documents, times a term frequency part: the count times k1 plus one, divided by the count plus k1 times a length factor, one minus b plus b times document length over average length. So rare terms dominate, repeats saturate, and long documents get discounted. Typical settings are k1 around 1.2 and b around 0.75. The Lucene version adds one inside the IDF log so the weight never goes negative for very common terms.
must_mention: length normalisation with b and avgdl

followups.q: What is BM25F?
followups.a: A version that scores separate fields such as title and body with their own weights and normalisation.

traps: Describing BM25 as plain TF IDF.

q: What do BM25's k1 and b parameters do? Show with numbers.
plain: k1 controls how quickly repeating a word stops helping, and b controls how much long documents are penalised. With the usual k1 of 1.2, a word appearing once in an average length document scores 1.0 times its rarity weight, twice scores 1.375, ten times 1.96, and it can never pass 2.2. With b at 0.75, a 13 word document containing 'refund policy' once each scored 0.78 against 1.19 for a 5 word document with the same words. Setting b to 0 would ignore length entirely.
deep: At $|D| = \mathrm{avgdl}$ the length factor is 1, so the term part is $f(k_1+1)/(f+k_1)$: with $k_1 = 1.2$, $f = 1, 2, 5, 10, 100$ give 1.0, 1.375, 1.774, 1.964, 2.174, approaching the cap $k_1 + 1 = 2.2$. Larger $k_1$ makes saturation slower (closer to raw TF); $k_1 = 0$ reduces to binary presence. $b$ scales $|D|/\mathrm{avgdl}$: $b = 1$ full normalisation (BM11), $b = 0$ none (BM15). Toy corpus (avgdl 7, IDF refund 0.357, policy 0.693): "refund policy for annual plans" (5 words) scores 1.189; a 13 word document with both terms once scores 0.777; "refund requests take five days" scores 0.404 (computed in Python). Tune on labelled queries; domains with long, repetitive documents often want different values.
say: k1 sets term frequency saturation. With k1 at 1.2 and an average length document, one occurrence gives 1.0 times the IDF, two give 1.375, ten give about 1.96, and the ceiling is k1 plus one, 2.2, so stuffing a keyword stops paying. b sets length normalisation: at 0.75, long documents are discounted, so in my toy corpus a thirteen word document with refund and policy once each scored 0.78, while a five word document with the same terms scored 1.19. At b of zero length is ignored, at one it's fully normalised against the average length.

followups.q: When would you lower b?
followups.a: When long documents are genuinely more relevant, for example long technical pages that cover a topic fully.

traps: Saying more occurrences of a term always increase the score proportionally.

q: Implement BM25 from scratch.
plain: The code counts, for each query word, how many documents contain it to get a rarity weight, then scores each document with the saturating, length adjusted count from the BM25 formula. On a four document toy corpus, the short document that contains both 'refund' and 'policy' wins, a longer document with the same words comes second, and a document about passwords scores zero. Writing it out once makes the formula easy to recall in an interview.
deep:
```python
import math
docs = ["refund policy for annual plans",
        "our refund policy explained in full detail with examples for every plan type",
        "refund requests take five days",
        "how to reset your password"]
toks = [d.split() for d in docs]
N = len(toks); avgdl = sum(map(len, toks)) / N

def idf(t):
    n = sum(t in d for d in toks)
    return math.log((N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5) + 1)

def bm25(q, d, k1=1.2, b=0.75):
    return sum(idf(t) * d.count(t) * (k1 + 1) /
               (d.count(t) + k1 * (1 - b + b * len(d) / avgdl)) for t in q)

q = "refund policy".split()
print([round(bm25(q, d), 3) for d in toks])   # [1.189, 0.777, 0.404, 0.0]
```
avgdl is 7; IDF is 0.357 for "refund" (in 3 of 4 documents) and 0.693 for "policy" (in 2 of 4). Production engines precompute document frequencies and lengths in the inverted index rather than scanning.
say: I compute document frequency for each query term across the corpus, turn it into IDF with the Lucene formula, log of N minus n plus a half over n plus a half, plus one. Then for each document, per query term, I take the count, multiply by k1 plus one, and divide by the count plus k1 times one minus b plus b times the document length over the average length, and sum IDF times that. On a toy corpus of four documents, the five word document containing refund and policy scored 1.19, a thirteen word one with the same words 0.78, and the password document zero.

followups.q: How does a real engine avoid scanning every document?
followups.a: It walks only the postings lists of the query terms and uses dynamic pruning to skip low scoring documents.

traps: Using raw term counts without the length normalisation.

q: Dense retrieval exists. Why do teams still run BM25?
plain: Keyword search is exact on names, codes, error messages and rare words, needs no training, runs fast on ordinary CPUs, and holds up on new kinds of text where learned models stumble. Its weakness is different words for the same idea: 'cancel my subscription' does not match 'terminate plan'. That weakness is exactly what meaning based search covers. So most strong systems run both and merge the results.
deep: BEIR (2021) made BM25 the zero shot baseline to beat: most dense and learned sparse models of the time averaged below it across 18 datasets (DPR minus 47.7 percent, DeepCT minus 27.9, SPARTA minus 20.3), with docT5query plus 1.6 and BM25 plus cross encoder plus 11. Efficiency: 20 ms per query on CPU with a 0.4 GB index for 1M DBPedia documents. It is exact on identifiers, rare entities and numbers, and needs no re embedding when models change. Weakness: vocabulary mismatch (synonyms, paraphrase), addressed by document or query expansion, or by hybrid retrieval with rank fusion.
say: Because it's good at exactly what embeddings are bad at. BM25 matches exact tokens, so product codes, error messages, names and numbers work, while dense vectors tend to blur them. It needs no training, runs fast on CPU with a small index, and it generalises: in BEIR, most dense retrievers of the time averaged below BM25 on unfamiliar datasets. Its weakness is vocabulary mismatch, cancel my subscription won't match terminate plan, which is where dense retrieval helps. So I run both and fuse the lists rather than choosing one.
must_mention: exact match on identifiers and rare terms
strong zero shot baseline in BEIR

followups.q: How do you reduce BM25's vocabulary mismatch without dense retrieval?
followups.a: Document expansion with generated queries, or query expansion with synonyms.

traps: Dismissing BM25 as obsolete.

topic: Hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion
q: Why combine keyword search and dense search instead of picking the better one?
plain: Because they fail on different questions. Keyword search misses paraphrases, like 'terminate plan' for 'cancel subscription'; dense search misses exact tokens, like an error code or a product number. Running both and merging the lists catches more of the right passages than either alone. The hard part is merging, because their scores are on completely different scales.
deep: BM25 and dense retrievers have complementary error profiles (lexical gap versus dense bottleneck losing exact tokens, rare entities and numbers), so their union has higher recall at a fixed depth than either. Score scales differ: BM25 is unbounded and query dependent, cosine lives in a narrow model specific band, so raw sums are meaningless. Options: per query score normalisation (min max, z score) plus a tuned weighted sum, or rank based fusion (RRF). Anthropic's contextual retrieval results show the gain: contextual embeddings alone 3.7 percent retrieval failure at 20, adding contextual BM25 brought it to 2.9 percent.
say: Because their failures are complementary. BM25 misses paraphrases and synonyms, while dense retrieval blurs exact tokens like error codes, product numbers and rare names. Merging the two lists catches more of the relevant passages at the same depth than either does alone; in Anthropic's contextual retrieval experiments, adding BM25 to embeddings cut the top twenty failure rate from about 3.7 to 2.9 percent. The practical problem is merging, because BM25 scores are unbounded and cosine scores sit in a narrow band, so I fuse by rank or normalise scores first.

followups.q: When would you skip hybrid?
followups.a: When a measured comparison shows one retriever adds nothing on your golden set, for example a corpus of short, keyword style product titles.

traps: Adding raw BM25 and cosine scores together.

topic: Hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion
q: What is reciprocal rank fusion? Write the formula.
plain: Reciprocal rank fusion merges ranked lists using only positions, not scores. Each document earns 1 divided by (60 plus its rank) from every list it appears in, and the documents are sorted by their total. A document ranked first in one list earns 1/61; a document ranked third and second in two lists earns 1/63 plus 1/62, which is about twice as much. It needs no tuning and no labelled data.
deep: Cormack, Clarke and Buttcher (SIGIR 2009): $\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r\in R} \frac{1}{k + r(d)}$, with $r(d)$ the rank of $d$ in list $r$ (absent documents contribute 0) and $k = 60$, fixed in a pilot and never changed. Credit decays slowly with rank, so lower ranked documents still count, and the constant damps any single list's top positions so an outlier system cannot dominate. Results: RRF beat Condorcet fusion, CombMNZ and the best individual system by 4 to 5 percent MAP on average across TREC experiments, and fusing LETOR 3 learning to rank baselines beat each of them. Properties: rank only (no calibration), computed incrementally list by list.
say: Reciprocal rank fusion scores each document by summing, over all the ranked lists it appears in, one divided by k plus its rank, with k usually sixty, then sorts by that sum. It only uses ranks, so it doesn't care that BM25 and cosine scores live on different scales, and it needs no training. A document near the top of several lists beats one that's first in only one list, which is usually what you want from fusion. The 2009 paper that introduced it found it beat Condorcet fusion, CombMNZ and the best single system by a few percent.
must_mention: sum of 1 over k plus rank

followups.q: What happens to documents missing from a list?
followups.a: They get nothing from that list; only lists containing them contribute.

traps: Thinking RRF needs calibrated scores.

topic: Hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion
q: Work through a reciprocal rank fusion example.
plain: Suppose keyword search ranks documents A, C, B, D and dense search ranks E, B, F, C. A is first in one list only, so it earns 1/61 = 0.0164. B is third and second, so it earns 1/63 + 1/62 = 0.0320. C is second and fourth, earning 0.0318. So B and C, which both methods liked, beat A and E, which each topped just one list.
say: Say BM25 returns A, C, B, D and the dense retriever returns E, B, F, C. With k of sixty, A gets one over sixty one, about 0.0164, from its single first place. B gets one over sixty three plus one over sixty two, about 0.032, and C gets one over sixty two plus one over sixty four, about 0.0318. So B and C, which both retrievers liked, end up first and second, ahead of A and E, which each topped only one list. If I drop k to one, top ranks dominate and A almost catches C, which shows what the constant does.

followups.q: How deep should each list be before fusion?
followups.a: Deep enough to feed the reranker, typically 50 to 100 per retriever.

traps: Fusing before deduplicating chunks from the same document.

topic: Hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion
q: What does the constant k do in reciprocal rank fusion, and does 60 matter?
plain: k controls how much the very top positions dominate. With a small k, being first in one list is worth a lot more than being fifth; with a large k, positions matter less and the fusion is closer to counting how many lists include a document. The original paper chose 60 in a pilot test and found the exact value was not critical. For example, with k equal to 1, rank 1 earns 0.5 and rank 5 earns 0.17; with k equal to 60, they earn 0.0164 and 0.0154.
deep: Term $1/(k + r)$: the ratio between rank 1 and rank $r$ credit is $(k + r)/(k + 1)$, which tends to 1 as $k$ grows. Small $k$ approximates "trust each list's top hit"; large $k$ approaches a count of appearances (CombSUM of indicators). Cormack et al.'s pilot (30 system runs, TREC topics 351 to 400) reported MAP 0.2072 at $k = 0$, 0.2123 at 10, 0.2145 at 60, 0.2147 at 80, 0.2098 at 500: near optimal at 60, flat across roughly 10 to 100. The constant also limits the impact of a single outlier system ranking a document first. Weighted RRF multiplies each list's contributions by a per list weight when one retriever is known to be stronger.
say: The constant controls how steeply credit falls with rank. The ratio between first place and rank r is k plus r over k plus one, so with a small k the top few positions dominate and fusion basically trusts each list's best hit, and with a large k positions barely matter and it's close to counting how many lists contain the document. Sixty came from a pilot in the original paper, and their table shows mean average precision almost flat from about ten to a hundred, so it's a sensible default rather than a magic number. I'd only tune it, or add per list weights, with labelled queries.
must_mention: controls decay of credit with rank

followups.q: Why does a moderate k resist outlier systems?
followups.a: One list placing a document first adds at most 1/(k+1), which cannot outweigh consistent moderate ranks from other lists.

traps: Presenting k = 60 as a theoretically derived optimum.

topic: Hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion
q: Reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted sum of normalised scores: how do you choose?
plain: Rank fusion needs no labelled data and stays stable when you swap models, so it is the safe default. A weighted blend of scores keeps information about how confident each retriever was, so it can do better, but only if you have labelled queries to tune the weight. For example, if dense search gives one passage a score far above all others, a score blend can trust it, while rank fusion treats it like any other first place. Decide with a measured comparison on your own queries.
deep: Score fusion: normalise per query (min max or z score), then $\alpha\, s_{dense} + (1 - \alpha)\, s_{bm25}$; it keeps margin information but is sensitive to score distributions that vary by query and model, and $\alpha$ must be tuned on labelled data and retuned when a model changes. RRF discards magnitudes: robust to calibration differences, no tuning, stable across model swaps, but blind to confidence. Weighted RRF is a middle ground. Choose by nDCG at 10 or recall at k on a labelled dev set, confirmed on held out queries with a paired test across queries (per query differences, bootstrap or permutation).
say: Without labelled queries I use RRF, since it only needs ranks, so differing score scales don't matter and it stays stable when I swap embedding models. With labels, a tuned weighted sum of per query normalised scores can win, because it keeps confidence: a dense score far above the rest means something that a rank throws away. The costs are tuning the weight and retuning whenever a model changes. I'd compare RRF, weighted RRF and score fusion on nDCG at ten with a paired test over the same queries, and keep the simplest one that isn't measurably worse.
must_mention: RRF needs no labels or calibration

followups.q: How would you pick alpha?
followups.a: Grid search on a labelled dev set by nDCG at 10, then confirm on held out queries.

traps: Normalising scores across the whole corpus instead of per query.

q: Why add a reranking stage, and what does it cost?
plain: The first search is tuned to find candidates quickly, so the best passage is often somewhere in the top hundred but not the top five. A reranker reads the question together with each candidate and rescores them, pushing the best ones up. In the BEIR benchmark, keyword search plus a reranker was the most accurate setup on average, about 11 percent better than keyword search alone. It took about 450 milliseconds per question on a GPU against 20 milliseconds for keyword search, which is why it only sees a short list.
deep: Two stage design: hybrid retrieve 100 to 150, cross encoder rerank, keep 5 to 20 for the generator. BEIR (2021): BM25 top 100 reranked by a cross encoder averaged plus 11 percent nDCG at 10 over BM25, the best method studied, at about 450 ms per query on a V100 (6.1 s on CPU) versus 20 ms for BM25 and under 20 ms for dense retrieval on GPU. Anthropic (2024) reranked the top 150 to 20 and cut retrieval failure at 20 from 2.9 to 1.9 percent. Cost drivers: one forward pass per candidate over $|q| + |d|$ tokens, attention quadratic in length, nothing precomputable. Levers: fewer candidates, smaller or distilled rerankers, GPU batching, caching repeated queries.
say: The first stage is optimised for recall, so the right chunk is often in the top hundred but not the top five. A cross encoder reads the query with each candidate and rescores it, and that pushes the right ones up. In BEIR, BM25 plus a cross encoder reranker was the most accurate setup, around eleven percent better than BM25 alone, but it took roughly four hundred fifty milliseconds per query on a GPU against twenty for BM25. So the reranker only ever sees a shortlist, and the number of candidates it scores is a latency knob I tune.
must_mention: rerank depth is a latency knob

followups.q: How do you cut reranking latency?
followups.a: Score fewer candidates, distil a smaller reranker, batch on GPU, cache scores for repeated queries.

traps: Reranking the whole corpus.

q: Your reranker improved nDCG, but many answers are still wrong. What do you check first?
plain: Check whether the right passage was ever in the list the reranker saw. A reranker can only reorder what it is given; if the first search missed the passage, nothing afterward can bring it back. So you measure the first stage on its own, for example the share of questions with a relevant passage in the top 100. If that number is fine, look at the reranker's ordering, and if that is fine too, the problem is in generation.
deep: Decompose by stage: first stage recall at the rerank depth (recall at 100) bounds everything; post rerank recall or nDCG at the context budget measures ordering; generation metrics (faithfulness, correctness) measure use of context. Low recall at 100: fix upstream (hybrid search, query rewriting, chunking, contextual headers, domain adapted embeddings, deeper candidate lists). High recall at 100 but low at 10: weak reranker, truncated long passages, domain mismatch. Retrieval fine but answer wrong: context ordering, conflicting sources, the model ignoring context. Slice the failures by query type since averages hide the failing category, and read the traces.
say: First, whether the right passage was ever in the candidate list. The reranker can't recover what the first stage missed, so I'd check recall at a hundred for the failing queries. If it's low, the fix is upstream: hybrid search, query rewriting, chunking or contextual headers. If recall at a hundred is high but the passage still isn't in the top ten, the reranker is the issue, maybe it's truncating long passages or is out of domain. And if the right passage is in the context and the answer is still wrong, it's generation, so I'd read those traces and look at ordering and conflicting sources.
must_mention: reranker cannot fix first stage misses
then ordering at the context budget

followups.q: How deep should the candidate list be?
followups.a: Deep enough that first stage recall has plateaued, balanced against reranker latency.

traps: Tuning the reranker when the first stage is the bottleneck.

q: When would you use an LLM as a reranker, and how can reranker scores help with refusal?
plain: A large language model can reorder passages by reading them all with the question, and it can be stronger than a small reranker on hard questions, but it costs far more per query. A good compromise is to use it on a very short list, or offline to create training labels for a cheaper reranker. Separately, the best reranker score is a useful signal for whether any passage really answers the question. If even the top passage scores very low, the system should hedge or say it cannot answer.
deep: LLM reranking (pointwise relevance prompts or listwise ordering of a shortlist) handles reasoning heavy relevance better but adds latency and cost proportional to candidates times passage length; use on a top 10 to 20, or offline to label data and distil into a cross encoder. Evidence gate: cross encoder scores are not probabilities by default; calibrate them (Platt or isotonic on labelled query passage pairs) and choose a threshold from the trade off between false answers and false refusals on a golden set with unanswerable questions. Combine with other signals (agreement between retrievers, a judge's answerability check).
say: An LLM reranker reads the query with a handful of passages and orders them, which can beat a small cross encoder on questions where relevance needs reasoning, but it's much slower and more expensive per query. So I'd use it on a very short list, or offline to label training data and distil into a cheaper reranker. Reranker scores are also a good evidence signal: if even the top candidate scores low, the system probably doesn't have the answer. I'd calibrate those scores on labelled pairs and pick a refusal threshold from the trade off between wrong answers and unnecessary refusals.

followups.q: Are cross encoder scores probabilities?
followups.a: Not by default; calibrate them on labelled pairs before using a fixed threshold.

traps: Using an uncalibrated raw reranker score as a fixed confidence cut off across domains.

topic: Query rewriting, HyDE and multi hop retrieval
q: How does a RAG system handle follow up questions in a conversation?
plain: It rewrites the follow up into a complete question before searching. The search index only sees the text it is given, and 'what about annual plans?' matches nothing useful on its own. A small model call uses the chat history to turn it into 'what is the refund policy for annual plans?'. The answering model still sees the full conversation; only the search uses the rewritten version.
deep: Retrieval sees only the query string, so references ("it", "that plan", "the second one") must be resolved first. A small LLM call rewrites the latest turn into a standalone query using recent history; optionally generate several rewrites and fuse results with RRF; extract structured filters (dates, product, region) into metadata filters. The generator gets the conversation plus retrieved context. Evaluate rewriting directly on a multi turn golden slice: recall at k with raw versus rewritten queries. Failure modes: dropping a constraint, inventing one, or carrying over a topic the user abandoned.
say: I rewrite the latest turn into a standalone query before retrieval, because the retriever only sees that string and what about the annual one matches nothing. A small model takes the recent history and produces something like refund policy for annual plans, and it can pull out filters too, like a date range or a product. The generator still sees the whole conversation, but search uses the rewrite. I'd test it on a slice of multi turn conversations, comparing recall with raw and rewritten queries, and watch for rewrites that drop or invent a constraint.

followups.q: What if the rewrite is wrong?
followups.a: Generate a few rewrites, retrieve for each and fuse, or keep the raw query as one of the lists.

traps: Embedding the whole chat history as the query.

topic: Query rewriting, HyDE and multi hop retrieval
q: Besides rewriting, what query side techniques improve retrieval?
plain: Several. Multi query expansion writes a few different phrasings, searches with each, and merges the results. Decomposition splits a compound question, like 'compare the refund rules for monthly and annual plans', into two simpler searches. Filter extraction turns phrases like 'since 2024' into exact metadata filters. Routing sends each question to the right source, for example a database for 'how many orders last week' and the document index for 'what is the return window'.
deep: Multi query: an LLM generates $n$ paraphrases, retrieve per paraphrase, fuse with RRF; raises recall at the cost of $n$ retrieval calls. Decomposition: split into sub questions retrieved and answered separately, then combined; needed for comparisons and multi part questions. Step back or abstraction queries retrieve background before specifics. Filter extraction: structured constraints into metadata filters rather than embedding them. Routing: a classifier or LLM picks the index, tool or SQL path. Each adds latency and its own failure mode, so evaluate per technique on slices that need it (comparisons, time bounded questions, aggregation questions).
say: A few. Multi query expansion has a model write several paraphrases, retrieves for each, and fuses the lists with RRF, which raises recall at the cost of more retrieval calls. Decomposition splits a compound question, like comparing refund rules for two plans, into sub questions retrieved separately. Filter extraction turns phrases like since 2024 or only HR policies into exact metadata filters instead of hoping the embedding captures them. And routing sends the question to the right backend, SQL for aggregates like orders last week, the document index for policy questions. Each adds latency, so I measure each on the slice of questions it targets.

followups.q: Why not embed the date constraint in the query text?
followups.a: Embeddings capture dates poorly; an exact metadata filter is reliable.

traps: Adding every technique at once without measuring each.

topic: Query rewriting, HyDE and multi hop retrieval
q: What is HyDE, and when would you use it?
plain: HyDE stands for hypothetical document embeddings. Instead of searching with the short question, the system asks a model to write a fake answer passage and searches for real documents that resemble it, because answers look more like documents than questions do. The fake passage may contain made up details, but only the real retrieved documents are used as evidence. It helps most in new domains with no training data, and it costs an extra model call before every search.
deep: Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan (2022): an instruction tuned LLM (InstructGPT) writes a hypothetical document for the query; an unsupervised contrastive encoder (Contriever) embeds it; retrieve real documents nearest that vector. The dense bottleneck keeps mostly the relevance pattern and drops hallucinated specifics, and retrieval grounds the result in the corpus. No training: it outperformed Contriever alone across web search, QA, fact verification and non English tasks (Swahili, Korean, Japanese). Use for zero shot domains and asymmetric query document styles. Costs and risks: LLM latency per query; for niche or proprietary facts the model's guess may point to the wrong region; mitigate by fusing with plain query results.
say: HyDE, hypothetical document embeddings: instead of embedding the user's short question, I ask a model to write a plausible answer passage, embed that, and retrieve real documents near it. Answers look more like documents than questions do, so the match improves, and the paper showed gains over an unsupervised dense retriever without training anything. The fake passage can contain invented details, but it's only used as a search key, the evidence comes from the real documents retrieved. I'd use it in zero shot settings, knowing it adds an LLM call before retrieval and can mislead on niche internal facts.
must_mention: fake text is only a search key

followups.q: How do you limit the risk of a misleading hypothetical?
followups.a: Fuse HyDE results with the plain query's dense and BM25 results using RRF.

traps: Thinking the hypothetical document is used as evidence in the answer.

topic: Query rewriting, HyDE and multi hop retrieval
q: How would you handle multi hop questions?
plain: Some questions need a chain of facts from different documents, where the second search depends on the first answer. 'Where was the author of Things Fall Apart born?' needs the author first (Chinua Achebe), then his birthplace. A single search cannot do that, so the system either splits the question into steps or searches, reads, and searches again. Every extra hop adds a chance of error, so hops need a limit and each step needs evidence.
deep: Approaches: decompose into sub questions and retrieve per step; iterative retrieval in a ReAct style loop (Thought, search, Observation, next search); reasoning models that decide when to search (Search-o1 triggers retrieval when the model expresses uncertainty; Search-R1 learns when to search with RL; both covered in CS329A Part 7). Benchmarks: HotpotQA, Bamboogle. Controls: hop limit, verification that each intermediate answer is supported by retrieved text, citations from every hop in the final answer, and evaluation of intermediate retrievals, not only the final answer.
say: Multi hop questions chain facts across documents, like where was the author of a given novel born, where the second search depends on the answer to the first. One retrieval call can't do that. I'd either decompose the question into sub questions and retrieve for each, or run an iterative loop where the model searches, reads, and issues the next query, which is ReAct with a search tool. Newer reasoning models can decide when to search on their own. The risks are compounding errors and loops, so I'd cap hops, check each intermediate answer is supported, and require citations from every hop.
must_mention: second query depends on first answer

followups.q: How do you evaluate it?
followups.a: Check retrieval and answers per hop as well as the final answer, on a multi hop golden slice.

traps: Expecting a larger top k to solve multi hop questions.

q: How do you enforce document permissions in a RAG system?
plain: Apply permission filters inside the search itself, so documents a user cannot see are never retrieved. Telling the model 'do not reveal documents this user cannot access' after putting them in its input is not access control; the model can still quote them, and a cleverly worded request can pull them out. Every chunk carries its access list from the moment it is indexed. For example, an HR salary document should never even reach the prompt for a sales employee's question.
deep: Attach ACLs, tenant ids and sensitivity labels to every chunk at ingestion; apply them as hard filters in the retrieval query, or keep separate indexes per tenant for strict isolation and simpler deletion. Prompt instructions are not a security boundary: the model can quote anything in context and prompt injection can extract it (OWASP 2025: LLM02 sensitive information disclosure, LLM08 vector and embedding weaknesses). Scope caches (semantic and response caches per permission set), agent memory and logs too. Test with negative golden cases asserting restricted content never appears for unauthorised users.
say: Permissions have to be enforced in retrieval, not in the prompt. Every chunk carries its access list and tenant from ingestion, and the search query filters on the user's permissions, so restricted documents never reach the model. Asking the model to ignore a document it has already been shown doesn't work, it can quote it, and a prompt injection can pull it out. I'd also scope caches and memory by permission set, because a semantic cache can serve one user's answer to another, and I'd keep test cases that check restricted content never shows up.

followups.q: Separate indexes or filters?
followups.a: Separate indexes per tenant for strict isolation and simpler deletion; filters when tenants are many and small.

traps: Relying on the system prompt to hide restricted documents.

q: What goes wrong when you combine a strict metadata filter with approximate vector search?
plain: If you search first and filter afterward, a strict filter throws away almost everything: with a filter that matches 1 percent of documents, the top 100 results leave about one survivor. If you filter first and then run a graph index like HNSW, most of the graph's points are excluded and the search can get stuck. The fixes are to fetch far more before filtering, to switch to exact search when the filtered set is small, or to use an engine that checks filters during the search.
deep: Post filtering: expected survivors $\approx k \times$ selectivity, so oversample by about $1/\text{selectivity}$. Pre filtering: exact search over the subset is fast and exact when it is small; for graph indexes, excluding most nodes breaks connectivity and greedy traversal stalls, cutting recall. Filter aware ANN evaluates predicates during traversal (engine dependent) but still degrades for very selective filters. Practical rules: estimate selectivity per query, switch to brute force below a subset size threshold, partition by high cardinality filters such as tenant, and benchmark recall specifically on filtered queries, which unfiltered benchmarks hide.
say: It depends where the filter runs. If I retrieve the top hundred and then filter, a filter that matches one percent of documents leaves about one result, so I'd need to oversample by about a hundred times. If I filter first and then run HNSW, most of the graph is excluded and greedy search can get stuck, so recall drops. What I'd actually do is estimate selectivity: small filtered subsets get exact search, large tenants get their own partition, otherwise an engine with filter aware search. And I'd measure recall on filtered queries separately, since unfiltered benchmarks hide this problem.

followups.q: What is filter selectivity?
followups.a: The share of documents that pass the filter; it decides which strategy works.

traps: Benchmarking ANN recall only on unfiltered queries.

q: How do you keep a RAG index fresh?
plain: Reindex only what changed, and track a version and date for every chunk. Hook into the source systems so that an edited policy page is embedded again within minutes instead of at the next monthly rebuild. Use dates in ranking or filtering for time sensitive questions, and give any cached answers an expiry time. A stale index is dangerous because it produces confident, correctly cited, wrong answers.
deep: Change data capture or scheduled diffs against source systems; re embed and reindex only changed documents; version and timestamp per chunk; recency boosts or filters when the query is time sensitive; TTL on response and semantic caches; monitor index lag (time from source change to searchable) as an operational metric. Embedding model upgrades require a full re embed into a new index version with an eval before switching. The failure is subtle: a stale passage yields an answer that is faithful to its context and cites a real source, so faithfulness metrics do not catch it; freshness needs its own golden cases (questions whose answer changed).
say: I'd hook into the source systems with change data capture or scheduled diffs and re embed only what changed, with a version and timestamp on every chunk. For time sensitive questions I'd filter or boost by recency, and any cached answers get a time to live. I'd track index lag, how long from a source change until it's searchable, as an operational metric. Embedding model upgrades mean a full re embed into a new index version that has to pass the eval before cutover. The reason this matters is that a stale index gives confident, correctly cited wrong answers, which faithfulness metrics won't catch.

followups.q: How do you test freshness?
followups.a: Golden cases whose correct answer changed recently, checked after each update cycle.

traps: Rebuilding the index monthly for a corpus that changes daily.

q: How do you delete a document properly from a RAG system?
plain: A document leaves copies in many places, and deletion has to reach all of them. Besides its chunks and vectors there are keyword index entries, generated summaries or context notes, cached answers that quoted it, agent memories, and test cases that reference it. Some indexes cannot remove items at all; HNSW in the FAISS library, for example, needs a marker that hides the item at search time and a later rebuild. A deletion request is only done when the document cannot reappear anywhere.
deep: Deletion must reach: chunks and their vectors, BM25 postings, LLM generated contextual headers or summaries, semantic and response caches, conversation and agent memory stores, eval references, and backups per retention policy. FAISS's IndexHNSW cannot remove vectors (removal would break the graph), so engines use tombstones filtered at query time plus periodic rebuilds or compaction; flat indexes in FAISS support remove but renumber ids. Keep a lineage table from document id to every derived artifact so deletion is a join rather than a search. Verify with golden cases asserting the deleted content never appears.
say: Deletion has to reach every copy a document leaves behind, not just its vectors: the chunks, the keyword postings, any generated summaries or contextual headers, cached answers, agent memories, and test cases that reference it. Some indexes can't remove items at all, FAISS's HNSW for example, so you tombstone the item, filter it at query time, and rebuild later. I'd keep a lineage table from each document id to everything derived from it, so deleting is a lookup rather than a hunt, and I'd have test cases that confirm deleted content never comes back.

followups.q: Why can HNSW not just remove a node?
followups.a: Removing nodes breaks graph connectivity that other nodes' searches rely on.

traps: Deleting the vector but leaving cached answers and summaries.

q: Why should a retracted or superseded document be filtered out rather than ranked lower?
plain: Because a lower rank still lets it into the answer. If a retracted medical paper drops from first to fifth, it can still be retrieved, quoted and cited, and the answer will look properly sourced while being wrong. Status like retracted, superseded or recalled is a rule about what is allowed, not a hint about relevance. So it belongs in a hard filter that applies the moment the status changes.
deep: Ranking features trade off against relevance; a strongly relevant retracted paper can outrank weaker valid ones, and once in context the generator treats it as evidence. Treat trust status as a correctness constraint: store it in metadata, maintain it from an authoritative registry, apply it as a hard filter at retrieval (and in caches), and propagate status changes immediately. Coverage of the registry bounds the guarantee: measure how many notices link to their target documents reliably. Evaluate with golden cases where the correct behaviour is to refuse or to cite only the non retracted source.
say: Because a demoted document can still be retrieved and cited. If a retracted paper is highly relevant, a ranking penalty might move it from first to fifth, it still lands in the context, and the generator treats it as evidence, producing an answer that looks well sourced and is wrong in a way the reader can't detect. Status like retracted or superseded is a rule about what's allowed, so I store it in metadata from an authoritative source, apply it as a hard filter in retrieval and caches, and update it immediately when it changes. I'd also measure how complete that status data is.
must_mention: hard filter at retrieval and caches

followups.q: What bounds the guarantee?
followups.a: How completely the status registry links notices to the documents they concern.

traps: Treating retraction as a ranking feature.

q: Define precision at k.
plain: Precision at k is the share of the top k results that are actually relevant. If a search returns 5 results and 2 of them answer the question, precision at 5 is 2 out of 5, or 0.40. It tells you how much of what you showed was useful. It ignores relevant documents that were never found and ignores order within the top k.
deep: $P@k = \frac{|\{\text{relevant}\} \cap \{\text{top } k\}|}{k}$. Example: graded relevance at ranks 1 to 10 of 0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0: $P@5 = 2/5 = 0.40$, $P@10 = 3/10 = 0.30$. Rank unaware within the cutoff and blind to missed relevant items (BEIR rejected it as its single metric for being rank unaware). For RAG it matters because irrelevant chunks in the context are distractors that can pull the generator off course and cost tokens. With graded relevance, choose a threshold for "relevant" and state it.
say: Precision at k is the number of relevant results in the top k divided by k. If I return five chunks and two are relevant, precision at five is 0.4. It tells me how clean the result list is, which matters for RAG because irrelevant chunks are distractors that cost tokens and can mislead the generator. But it ignores order inside the top k and says nothing about relevant documents I never retrieved, so I never report it alone. I pair it with recall at k and a rank aware metric like nDCG.
must_mention: relevant in top k over k

followups.q: How do you count graded relevance?
followups.a: Pick a grade threshold for relevant and state it, or use nDCG which uses grades directly.

traps: Reporting precision alone as retrieval quality.

q: Define recall at k, and why is it usually the first retrieval metric for RAG?
plain: Recall at k is the share of all the relevant documents for a question that made it into the top k results. If a question has 4 relevant passages and 3 appear in the top 10, recall at 10 is 0.75. For RAG it comes first because the model can only use the passages it receives, so recall at the number of chunks you send caps the whole system's accuracy. You measure it at exactly the k you put in the prompt.
deep: $R@k = \frac{|\{\text{relevant}\} \cap \{\text{top } k\}|}{R}$ where $R$ is the number of relevant items for the query. Example (4 relevant items, hits at ranks 2, 4, 6): $R@5 = 2/4 = 0.50$, $R@10 = 3/4 = 0.75$. RAG relevance: the generator cannot use unretrieved evidence, so recall at the context budget is an upper bound on answerable questions; recall at the rerank depth (say 100) bounds what the reranker can recover. Anthropic's contextual retrieval reports 1 minus recall at 20 as its failure rate. Requires knowing all relevant items, so incomplete judgments inflate or deflate it.
say: Recall at k is the fraction of all relevant documents for a query that appear in the top k. If there are four relevant passages and three show up in the top ten, recall at ten is 0.75. For RAG it's my first metric because the generator can only use what it receives, so recall at the exact number of chunks I put in the prompt is a ceiling on how many questions the system can answer from evidence. I also track recall at the rerank depth, like a hundred, because that bounds what the reranker can fix.
must_mention: relevant in top k over all relevant

followups.q: What is the weakness of recall at k?
followups.a: It needs all relevant items to be known; incomplete labels distort it, and it ignores order within k.

traps: Measuring recall at 100 when only 5 chunks are sent to the model.

q: What are hit rate and mean reciprocal rank?
plain: Hit rate at k asks a yes or no question per query: is at least one relevant result in the top k? Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by the position of the first relevant result, so a first relevant hit at position 2 gives 0.5 and no hit gives 0. Mean reciprocal rank (MRR) averages that over all queries. Across three queries whose first hits are at positions 1, 2 and never, MRR is (1 + 0.5 + 0) divided by 3, which is 0.5.
deep: Hit@k (success at k) $= \mathbb{1}[\exists\, i \le k: rel_i > 0]$, averaged over queries. $\mathrm{RR} = 1/\mathrm{rank}_{first}$ (0 if none), $\mathrm{MRR} = \frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_q \mathrm{RR}_q$. Both are binary in relevance and care only about the first hit, so they fit navigational or single answer queries (one passage suffices). MRR at 10 truncates: no hit in the top 10 counts 0. ColBERT and MS MARCO report MRR at 10. Weakness: insensitive to the second and later relevant items, which matter when an answer needs several passages.
say: Hit rate at k is binary per query, did any relevant result appear in the top k, averaged over queries. Reciprocal rank is one over the position of the first relevant result, so first hit at position two gives a half, and no hit gives zero; mean reciprocal rank averages that across queries. So three queries with first hits at one, two and never give an MRR of 0.5. Both only care about the first relevant result, which suits single answer questions, but they ignore whether the second and third supporting passages were found, which matters for multi passage answers.
must_mention: hit rate is any relevant in top k
reciprocal rank 1 over first hit position

followups.q: When is MRR the right metric?
followups.a: When one relevant result is enough, like navigational or single fact questions.

traps: Using MRR for questions that need several passages.

q: Define average precision and MAP.
plain: Average precision looks at each position where a relevant result appears, computes the precision up to that point, and averages those numbers, dividing by the total number of relevant documents so missed ones count as zero. It rewards putting all the relevant documents near the top. With relevant hits at positions 2, 4 and 6 and four relevant documents in total, the precisions are 1/2, 2/4 and 3/6, so average precision is 1.5 divided by 4, which is 0.375. MAP is the mean of that over queries.
deep: $\mathrm{AP} = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{i:\,rel_i > 0} P@i$, $\mathrm{MAP} = \frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_q \mathrm{AP}_q$. Example: hits at ranks 2, 4, 6 with $R = 4$: $(0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5)/4 = 0.375$. Some implementations divide by the number of relevant items retrieved (here 3, giving 0.5), which does not penalise misses: state the denominator. AP is binary in relevance and approximates the area under the precision recall curve for the ranking. Cormack et al. (2009) reported RRF results in MAP. BEIR rejected MAP as its single metric because it cannot use graded judgments.
say: Average precision takes the precision at each rank where a relevant document appears and averages those values, dividing by the total number of relevant documents, so a relevant document never retrieved contributes zero. In my example, hits at ranks two, four and six each have precision one half, and with four relevant documents total that's 1.5 over 4, or 0.375. MAP is the mean over queries. Two things to say in an interview: it treats relevance as binary, and some code divides by relevant documents retrieved instead, which would give 0.5 here and hide the miss.

followups.q: How does AP relate to the precision recall curve?
followups.a: It approximates the area under it for a single ranking.

traps: Dividing by relevant items retrieved and silently ignoring misses.

q: What are DCG and nDCG?
plain: DCG gives each result credit for how relevant it is, then shrinks that credit the further down the list it appears, and adds everything up. nDCG divides DCG by the best possible DCG for that query, so a perfect ranking scores 1 and scores are comparable across queries. Unlike precision or MRR, it uses graded relevance, so a highly relevant result at the top counts more than a partly relevant one. It is the standard single metric in retrieval benchmarks such as BEIR, at a cutoff of 10.
deep: $\mathrm{DCG@k} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{g(rel_i)}{\log_2(i+1)}$, with linear gain $g = rel$ or exponential gain $g = 2^{rel} - 1$ (which rewards top grades more). $\mathrm{nDCG@k} = \mathrm{DCG@k}/\mathrm{IDCG@k}$ where IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ordering of **all judged relevant items** for the query, including ones the system never retrieved. Discount: rank 1 counts fully, rank 2 counts $1/\log_2 3 = 0.631$, rank 3 counts $1/\log_2 4 = 0.5$. BEIR chose nDCG at 10 because precision and recall are rank unaware and MRR and MAP are binary, while nDCG handles binary and graded judgments.
say: DCG sums the gain of each result divided by log base two of its rank plus one, so rank one counts fully, rank two about sixty three percent, rank three half. The gain is the relevance grade, or two to the grade minus one if you want top grades to count more. nDCG divides by the ideal DCG, the same sum for the best possible ordering of every judged relevant document, so a perfect ranking scores one and queries are comparable. It's the standard benchmark metric, BEIR used nDCG at ten, because it's rank aware and handles graded relevance.
must_mention: gain over log2 of rank plus one

followups.q: Why did BEIR choose nDCG at 10?
followups.a: It is rank aware and works for both binary and graded judgments.

traps: Building the ideal DCG from the retrieved list only.

q: Compute nDCG at 10 for a ranked list with graded relevance.
plain: Take ten results graded 0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, where the query has four relevant documents in total graded 3, 2, 2 and 1, one of which was never retrieved. The actual score adds 3 divided by about 1.58, plus 2 divided by about 2.32, plus 1 divided by about 2.81, giving 3.11. The best possible ordering of all four relevant documents scores 5.69. So nDCG at 10 is 3.11 divided by 5.69, about 0.55.
deep: Linear gain: $\mathrm{DCG} = \frac{3}{\log_2 3} + \frac{2}{\log_2 5} + \frac{1}{\log_2 7} = 1.893 + 0.861 + 0.356 = 3.110$. Ideal over 3, 2, 2, 1: $\frac{3}{1} + \frac{2}{\log_2 3} + \frac{2}{2} + \frac{1}{\log_2 5} = 3 + 1.262 + 1 + 0.431 = 5.693$. $\mathrm{nDCG@10} = 0.5464$. Exponential gain ($2^{rel} - 1$): DCG 6.065, IDCG 10.823, nDCG 0.5603. Verified with scikit-learn: `ndcg_score(y_true, y_score, k=10)` returns 0.5464 when the missed grade 2 item is appended to `y_true` with the lowest score, because sklearn builds the ideal ranking from the `y_true` you pass. Same list: P@5 0.40, R@10 0.75, RR 0.50, AP 0.375.
say: The hits are at ranks two, four and six with grades three, two and one. DCG is three over log two of three, plus two over log two of five, plus one over log two of seven, which is about 1.89 plus 0.86 plus 0.36, so 3.11. The ideal orders all four judged documents, grades three, two, two, one, at the top, giving about 5.69, including the grade two document the system never found. So nDCG at ten is about 0.55. With exponential gain it's 0.56. I checked it against scikit learn, which only matches if you include the missed document in the labels.
must_mention: sklearn needs the missed item in y_true

followups.q: What would nDCG be if you built the ideal from retrieved items only?
followups.a: 3.110 over the ideal of 3, 2, 1 (4.762), about 0.65, overstating quality by hiding the miss.

traps: Forgetting the missed relevant document when computing the ideal.

q: Implement precision, recall, reciprocal rank, AP and nDCG in Python and check them against scikit-learn.
plain: The code computes each metric for one ranked list directly from its definition and prints them, then calls scikit-learn's ndcg_score as an independent check. The check only agrees if the relevant document the system missed is included in the labels passed to scikit-learn, which is a useful reminder of how the ideal ranking is built. Writing this once makes the definitions stick and catches off by one errors in rank discounts.
deep:
```python
import math
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import ndcg_score

retrieved = [0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
judged = [3, 2, 2, 1]; R = len(judged)
p5 = sum(r > 0 for r in retrieved[:5]) / 5
r10 = sum(r > 0 for r in retrieved[:10]) / R
rr = next(1 / (i + 1) for i, r in enumerate(retrieved) if r > 0)
hits = [i for i, r in enumerate(retrieved) if r > 0]
ap = sum(sum(r > 0 for r in retrieved[:i + 1]) / (i + 1) for i in hits) / R
dcg = lambda g: sum(x / math.log2(i + 2) for i, x in enumerate(g))
ndcg = dcg(retrieved) / dcg(sorted(judged, reverse=True))
print(p5, r10, rr, ap, round(ndcg, 4))            # 0.4 0.75 0.5 0.375 0.5464
y_true = np.array([retrieved + [2]])              # append the missed relevant doc
y_score = np.array([list(range(11, 1, -1)) + [0]])
print(round(ndcg_score(y_true, y_score, k=10), 4))  # 0.5464
```
Note `log2(i + 2)` for zero based index $i$ equals $\log_2(\text{rank} + 1)$.
say: I compute each metric straight from its definition on one ranked list of graded relevances: precision at five as relevant in the top five over five, recall at ten over all four relevant documents, reciprocal rank from the first hit, average precision as the mean precision at each hit divided by all relevant documents, and nDCG with a log two discount over the ideal ordering of all judged documents. Then I cross check nDCG with scikit learn's ndcg score. It matched at 0.5464 only after I appended the missed relevant document to the labels, because scikit learn builds the ideal from whatever labels you give it.
must_mention: zero based index uses log2 of i plus 2

followups.q: How would you aggregate across queries?
followups.a: Compute per query, then take the mean, and keep the per query values for paired tests.

traps: Off by one in the rank discount.

q: Compare MRR, MAP and nDCG. When would you use each?
plain: MRR only looks at the first relevant result, so it suits questions where one good answer is enough. MAP rewards getting every relevant document near the top but treats relevance as simply yes or no. nDCG also rewards ordering very relevant documents above partly relevant ones. For a RAG system you would usually report recall at the number of chunks sent, plus nDCG at 10 for ordering, and MRR when one passage normally answers the question.
deep: MRR: binary, first hit only; navigational or single answer queries. MAP: binary, every relevant item, approximates area under the precision recall curve; good when completeness matters (legal discovery style). nDCG: graded and position discounted, normalised per query; BEIR's single metric at 10. In the worked example: RR 0.50, AP 0.375, nDCG@10 0.546. For RAG: recall at the context budget (coverage), nDCG at 10 (ordering with grades), MRR when one passage suffices; plus answer level metrics downstream. All are per query averages, so compare systems with paired tests across queries.
say: MRR only looks at the first relevant result, so it fits cases where one good answer is enough. MAP averages precision at every relevant hit, so it rewards getting all relevant documents high, but treats relevance as binary. nDCG handles graded relevance with a position discount, which is why BEIR used nDCG at ten as its single metric across very different datasets. For RAG, I'd report recall at the context budget for coverage, nDCG at ten for ordering, and MRR if a single passage usually answers the question, and then answer level metrics on top.
must_mention: recall at context budget for RAG

followups.q: Which metric would you report to a product team?
followups.a: Recall at k and hit rate in plain words, plus answer level accuracy, with nDCG as the engineering metric.

traps: Using MAP with graded judgments and silently binarising them.

q: Your new retriever finds good documents that were never labelled. How do you evaluate it fairly?
plain: Relevance labels are usually collected by having people judge the results of older systems, and anything nobody judged is assumed irrelevant. A new system that finds different good documents gets marked down for gaps in the labels, not for mistakes. The fix is to measure how many of its top results were never judged, get those judged, and recompute the scores for every system. The BEIR benchmark found exactly this bias against non keyword systems.
deep: Qrels come from pooling: annotators judge candidates from existing systems; unjudged documents count as non relevant. BEIR showed lexical bias from BM25 style pools (for example BioASQ candidates retrieved by term matching) and, after manually judging holes in TREC-COVID, found significant improvements for non lexical systems. It reports Hole at 10, the share of unjudged items in the top 10 (BM25 6.4 percent versus higher for neural systems). Remedies: report Hole at k; judge the new system's unjudged top k with humans or a calibrated judge and recompute for all systems; treat metrics on incomplete pools with caution.
say: The old labels were made by pooling results from older systems, and everything nobody judged counts as irrelevant, so a retriever that finds different good documents gets punished for holes rather than errors. BEIR showed this with BM25 style pooling, and when they judged the holes in TREC COVID the non lexical systems' scores went up. So I'd report how much of each system's top ten is unjudged, BEIR calls it hole at ten, get those documents judged, by people or a calibrated judge, for every system, and recompute before comparing.
must_mention: judge the holes for all systems

followups.q: Why judge holes for all systems, not just the new one?
followups.a: Otherwise the old systems' unjudged documents still count as misses, biasing the comparison the other way.

traps: Declaring the old system better because the new one retrieved unjudged documents.

q: How do you decide whether one retriever is really better than another on a test set?
plain: Compare them question by question on the same set, not just by their averages. Some questions are much harder than others, and that variation is far bigger than the difference between two systems, so averages alone can mislead. A paired test looks at the per question differences, for example with a bootstrap that resamples questions many times to see how often system B beats A. If B wins by 0.02 nDCG on average but the interval includes zero, you have not shown it is better.
deep: Compute the metric per query for both systems on identical queries; analyse differences $d_q = m_B(q) - m_A(q)$. Paired bootstrap: resample queries with replacement, recompute the mean difference, report a confidence interval; or a paired permutation (randomisation) test, or a paired t test / Wilcoxon signed rank on $d_q$. Pairing removes query difficulty variance. Also slice by query type, since a gain on one slice can hide a loss on another. With few queries (tens), only large effects are detectable; plan the test set size from the smallest difference worth detecting. The same logic gives McNemar's test for paired pass/fail outcomes later.
say: I compare per query, paired, on the same set. Query difficulty varies far more than the gap between two systems, so comparing two averages can easily mislead. I compute nDCG or recall for each query under both systems, take the differences, and run a paired bootstrap, resampling queries many times to get a confidence interval on the mean difference, or a paired permutation test. If the interval includes zero, I haven't shown an improvement. I also look at slices, because a gain on one query type can hide a loss on another.

followups.q: How many queries do you need?
followups.a: Enough to detect the smallest difference you care about; tens of queries only detect large effects.

traps: Declaring a winner from two averages on 30 queries.

q: What is the difference between faithfulness and correctness in a RAG answer?
plain: A faithful answer says only what the retrieved text supports. A correct answer matches the truth. They can disagree in both directions: an answer copied faithfully from an outdated policy page is faithful but wrong, and a true answer that came from the model's memory is correct but not faithful. You need both, so you measure them separately. A third property, answer relevance, asks whether the answer addresses the question at all.
deep: Faithfulness (groundedness): every claim entailed by the provided context; RAGAS measures supported statements over statements. Correctness: agreement with a reference or ground truth. Failure modes are independent: stale or wrong retrieval gives faithful but incorrect answers; parametric knowledge gives correct but ungrounded answers, a problem when provenance is required and a risk because the next memory based answer may be wrong with no citation to expose it. Answer relevance: addresses the question completely without padding. Measure faithfulness with claim level NLI or a calibrated judge, correctness against references on a golden set, relevance with a rubric.
say: Faithfulness asks whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context. Correctness asks whether the answer is actually true. They come apart both ways. If retrieval pulls an outdated policy and the model summarises it accurately, it's faithful and wrong. If the model ignores the context and answers from memory, it might be right but it's unfaithful, and next time its memory will be wrong with no citation to catch it. So I measure both: faithfulness at the claim level against the context, and correctness against reference answers on a golden set.
must_mention: stale passage gives faithful but wrong

followups.q: Where does answer relevance fit?
followups.a: A third axis: whether the answer addresses the question, regardless of support or truth.

traps: Treating a high faithfulness score as proof the answers are right.

q: The model cites sources. How do you know the citations really support the claims?
plain: You check them after the answer is written. Each sentence carries the id of the passage it cites, and a checker compares the sentence with that passage to see whether the passage actually says it. Models often attach a real source to a sentence that the source does not support, so the presence of a citation proves nothing. Two numbers summarise the result: citation precision, the share of citations that really support their sentence, and citation recall, the share of claims that have support.
deep: Mechanics: chunk ids in the prompt; structured output with a citation per sentence; post hoc verification with an NLI model (premise: cited span, hypothesis: claim) or a calibrated LLM judge; check that cited ids exist and were in the context (catches fabricated citations). Citation precision = supporting citations over citations; citation recall = claims with a supporting citation over claims. Eugene Yan (2024) reports a fine tuned NLI factual consistency model raising ROC AUC from 0.56 to 0.85, making NLI a cheap, fast checker relative to an LLM call per claim. Unsupported sentences are removed, flagged or trigger regeneration.
say: I verify them after generation. Each sentence carries the id of the chunk it cites, and a checker, either an NLI model or a calibrated judge, asks whether that chunk actually entails the sentence. That gives citation precision, the share of citations that really support their sentence, and citation recall, the share of claims that have support at all. I also check every cited id was actually in the context, which catches invented citations. Unsupported sentences get dropped or flagged. A fine tuned NLI model is often good enough and far cheaper than an LLM call per claim.
must_mention: cited ids must exist in context

followups.q: Why not trust the model to cite correctly?
followups.a: Models attach plausible citations to unsupported sentences; only checking the span measures grounding.

traps: Counting the presence of a citation as grounding.

q: How do you make a RAG system refuse when the evidence is missing, and how do you test it?
plain: Give the system a signal for whether the retrieved text really answers the question, and a threshold below which it says it cannot answer. Signals include the top reranker score, whether the two search methods agree, and a quick check asking 'does this context contain the answer?'. Test it with questions whose answers are not in the documents, and count two mistakes: answering when it should have refused, and refusing when the answer was there. Lowering one raises the other, so choose based on which mistake costs more.
deep: Evidence sufficiency gate: features such as the top calibrated reranker score, agreement between dense and BM25 lists, and an answerability judgment; plus a prompt that explicitly permits "the sources do not answer this". Evaluate as selective prediction on a golden set with unanswerable questions: false answer rate (answered, should refuse) versus false refusal rate (refused, evidence existed); sweeping the threshold traces a risk coverage curve; choose the operating point from error costs (in medicine or law a wrong cited answer is worse than a refusal). Monitor refusal rate online; a sudden rise usually means retrieval broke.
say: I build an explicit evidence gate. Signals like the best reranker score, whether the dense and keyword retrievers agree, and a quick judge asking does this context contain the answer, feed a threshold that I calibrate on labelled examples, and the prompt explicitly allows saying the sources don't cover it. To test it, the golden set needs unanswerable questions, and I count two errors: answering when it should have refused, and refusing when the evidence was there. The threshold trades one for the other, so I set it by which mistake is costlier for the product.
must_mention: unanswerable cases in the golden set

followups.q: What does a sudden rise in refusals in production suggest?
followups.a: Retrieval broke: an index, filter or embedding change, or new topics the corpus lacks.

traps: A golden set with no unanswerable questions.

topic: The RAG pipeline end to end
q: Walk me through what happens between a user pressing enter and getting an answer from a RAG system over a 200 page PDF.
plain: Before the question, the PDF was parsed with its tables kept intact, split into chunks along its sections, labelled with page numbers, and indexed for both meaning search and keyword search. When the user presses enter, the question is rewritten if it depends on earlier turns, both indexes return about 100 candidates, the lists are merged, and a reranker picks the best 10 or so. The model answers from those chunks with page citations, a check confirms each citation supports its sentence, and if the evidence is weak the system says the document does not cover it. Every step is logged so failures can be traced.
deep: Offline: parse (layout, tables, headers and footers, OCR if scanned), chunk structure aware with tables whole, attach doc id, page, section path, version; embed and BM25 index. Online: rewrite with history; extract filters; hybrid retrieve about 100; RRF fusion; cross encoder rerank to about 10; assemble prompt with chunk ids and pages within a token budget; generate with a citation per claim; verify citations (NLI or calibrated judge); evidence gate (answer, hedge, refuse); log trace. Stage metrics: recall at 100, nDCG at 10, faithfulness and citation precision, false answer rate on unanswerables, p95 latency and cost. Also say the alternative: one 200 page PDF may fit in a long context window, so compare against long context with caching first.
say: Before the question arrives, the PDF has been parsed, keeping tables intact, split into chunks along its sections, tagged with page and section, and indexed both as embeddings and in a keyword index. When the user hits enter, I rewrite the question if it depends on earlier turns, retrieve about a hundred candidates from both indexes, fuse them, and rerank down to about ten with a cross encoder. The model answers from those with page citations, a check confirms the citations support the claims, and if the evidence is weak it says the document doesn't cover it. Every step is logged. I'd also mention that one PDF might simply fit in context.

followups.q: Which number would you look at first if answers were bad?
followups.a: Retrieval recall at the context budget on a golden set.

followups.q: Would you even retrieve for one 200 page PDF?
followups.a: It might fit in context; compare long context with caching against RAG on a golden set.

traps: Describing only embed, search and generate.
