q: What is a regression gate for an LLM application, and what should it check?
plain: A regression gate is an automatic check in the release pipeline that blocks a change if quality gets worse. A good gate has layers: basic checks that must always pass, such as valid output format and no leaked secrets; critical test cases with zero tolerance, such as refusing when there is no evidence; overall scores compared with the last released version on the same cases, within a small tolerance; and limits on latency and cost per request. For example, a prompt change that improves average quality but breaks one safety case is still blocked.
deep: Tiers: (1) deterministic assertions that must all pass (schemas, citation format, no leaked identifiers or secrets, refusal on known out of scope requests); (2) must pass golden cases with zero tolerance (safety blocks, refusal on missing evidence, high value flows); (3) aggregate metrics versus the last released baseline on identical cases (pass rate, faithfulness, recall at k) with a tolerance and a paired statistical check; (4) budgets (p95 latency, tokens and cost per case). Reproducibility: pin model, judge model and version, judge prompt and temperature, index version; cache system outputs by input hash; sample several runs for known flaky cases. Report: per slice results and the list of regressed cases, not only the aggregate.
say: A regression gate is the eval suite turned into a release rule. Mine has tiers: deterministic checks that must all pass, like schema validity, citation format and no leaked secrets; must pass golden cases with zero tolerance, like refusing when evidence is missing or blocking unsafe requests; aggregate metrics compared with the last release on the same cases, with a tolerance and a paired test; and budgets for p95 latency and cost per case. To make it reproducible I pin the model, judge, judge prompt and index versions and cache outputs. The report lists every regressed case, not just the average.
must_mention: must pass cases with zero tolerance
metrics versus last release on same cases

followups.q: Why pin the judge version?
followups.a: A judge upgrade changes scores by itself, which would look like a system regression or improvement.

traps: Gating only on one average score.

q: Your eval pass rate dropped 5 points on 200 cases. Is that a real regression? Work it out.
plain: Compare the old and new versions on the same cases and look only at cases where they disagree. Say 150 cases pass under both, 18 passed before but now fail, 8 failed before but now pass, and 24 fail under both. The old pass rate is 84 percent and the new is 79 percent. A standard paired test on the 18 versus 8 split gives a p value of about 0.076, so by statistics alone the drop could be chance. But you still read all 18 broken cases, any broken critical case blocks the release, and you never lower a threshold just to make the change pass.
deep:
Exact McNemar test: under no change, discordant pairs split 50/50, so test $c$ new only passes out of $b + c$ discordant with a binomial(0.5) test. Here $b = 18$, $c = 8$: $p = 0.076$ (scipy `binomtest(8, 26, 0.5)`).

```python
from scipy.stats import binomtest
both_pass, old_only, new_only, both_fail = 150, 18, 8, 24
n = both_pass + old_only + new_only + both_fail
print((both_pass + old_only) / n, (both_pass + new_only) / n)   # 0.84 0.79
print(round(binomtest(new_only, old_only + new_only, 0.5).pvalue, 3))   # 0.076
```
Gate logic combines a fixed tolerance (block if the new rate is more than 2 points below baseline), zero tolerance must pass cases, and the statistical test; small sets cannot detect 5 point changes reliably, so tolerance rules and case review carry weight. Never relax thresholds to get a change through: find the cause or document the failure, and keep known failures visible in the report, since a suite that always passes measures nothing.
say: I'd compare paired outcomes on the same cases. Say a hundred fifty pass under both versions, eighteen regressed, eight improved, and twenty four fail under both, so the pass rate went from eighty four to seventy nine. McNemar's test only looks at the disagreeing cases: under no real change they'd split evenly, and eighteen versus eight gives a p value of about 0.076. So statistically it might be noise, but I wouldn't ship on that alone. Any regressed must pass case blocks, a fixed tolerance blocks a drop this size, and someone reads all eighteen regressions. And I'd never lower the threshold to get the change through.
must_mention: paired outcomes on the same cases
tolerance and must pass cases still block

followups.q: Why not compare the two pass rates with an unpaired test?
followups.a: The cases are shared, so pairing removes case difficulty variance; an unpaired test wastes power.

traps: Shipping because p is above 0.05 without reading the regressed cases.
Lowering the gate threshold to make the build green.

q: How do you keep LLM eval runs reproducible enough to gate releases?
plain: Fix everything that could change the score other than the change you are testing. Pin the exact model and judge versions, the judge's prompt and temperature, and the index the system retrieves from. Store each system output keyed by its input, so reruns of unchanged cases cost nothing and do not drift. For cases known to flip randomly, run them several times and judge the pass rate. For example, if a judge model is silently upgraded, all scores can shift by several points with no change to your system.
deep: Sources of nondeterminism: sampling (temperature, top p), model and judge version upgrades, judge prompt edits, index or corpus changes, tool and API responses, time dependent content. Controls: pinned model identifiers, temperature 0 or fixed seeds where supported, versioned judge prompts and rubric, versioned index snapshots, recorded tool responses for replay, output caching by input hash, repeated sampling (for example 3 to 5 runs) on flaky cases with pass rates and pass hat k, and an A/A run (old versus old) to measure the noise floor before trusting any difference. Record every version in the run artefact so a score is traceable to a command and its inputs.
say: I pin everything except the thing I'm testing: exact model and judge versions, the judge prompt and temperature, the index snapshot, and recorded tool responses for replay. I cache system outputs by input hash so reruns are free and stable. Cases known to be flaky get several samples, and I report their pass rate rather than one draw. I also run an A A comparison, old against old, to see how much the score moves from noise alone, before trusting any difference. And every run records its versions, so any number in a report traces back to a command and inputs.
must_mention: pin model, judge, prompt and index versions
A/A run for the noise floor

followups.q: What is an A/A run?
followups.a: Running the same system twice through the eval to measure score variation with no real change.

traps: Letting the judge model auto update between baseline and candidate runs.

q: What is benchmark contamination, and how do you detect and avoid it?
plain: Contamination means test questions, or close copies of them, ended up in a model's training data, so a high score shows memory rather than skill. Signs include the model reproducing reference answers word for word, scores dropping sharply when questions are reworded, and much better results on questions published before the model's training cutoff than after. Defences include testing on questions written after the cutoff, keeping test sets private, and rewording or changing the numbers in questions. SWE-bench, for example, was designed so new tasks can keep being collected from recent GitHub issues.
deep: Public benchmarks (MMLU knowledge, AIME reasoning, SWE-bench coding, HarmBench safety, tau-bench agents, surveyed in CME295 Lecture 8) leak through web scraped pretraining data. Detection: verbatim reproduction of references, sharp drops on paraphrased or perturbed items (renamed variables, changed numbers, reordered options), performance gaps between pre cutoff and post cutoff items, n gram overlap checks when you control the training corpus, membership inference style tests when you do not. Avoidance: time split evaluation (SWE-bench can evaluate on issues created after a model's training date), private or rotating test sets, canary strings in published data so training pipelines can exclude it. Related decay: saturation, when top systems cluster at the ceiling and differences become noise.
say: Contamination is when benchmark items or close paraphrases were in the training data, so the score measures memory. Signs are verbatim reproduction of reference answers, sharp drops when items are paraphrased or numbers changed, and much better performance on items from before the training cutoff than after. To avoid it: time splits, evaluating on items created after the cutoff, which SWE bench supports by collecting new GitHub issues; private or rotating test sets; canary strings so training pipelines can exclude the data; and perturbation tests. Benchmarks also saturate, once everyone is near the ceiling the differences are noise.

followups.q: Why can SWE-bench resist contamination?
followups.a: Its pipeline can collect fresh tasks from issues created after a model's training cutoff.

traps: Trusting a leaderboard jump without checking for contamination.

q: How can your own golden set become contaminated?
plain: Your private test set leaks too, just more quietly. If you keep tuning prompts until the golden set passes, the prompt slowly memorises those cases and the score stops predicting real performance. Copying golden cases into few shot examples, fine tuning on logs that include eval inputs, or writing reference answers with the same model you are testing all leak the answers. For example, a team that tuned against the same 100 cases for six months may see 95 percent offline while users complain.
deep: Leak paths: iterative prompt tuning on the full set (overfitting by selection), few shot examples drawn from eval cases, fine tuning data containing eval inputs or outputs, references generated by the system under test or its family (inflating agreement), judges calibrated on the test split, and documents added to the corpus specifically to make cases pass. Controls: a held out test split used rarely and never for tuning (Hamel's dev versus test discipline for judges applies equally to systems), dedup checks between training or few shot pools and eval sets, provenance tags per case, fresh production derived cases added regularly, and monitoring whether offline trends still predict online outcomes. BEIR's lexical pooling bias is the benchmark scale analogue: how the labels were built shapes which systems look good.
say: Quietly, through selection. If I tune prompts against the full golden set for months, the prompt effectively memorises those cases and the score stops predicting production. Other leaks are pulling few shot examples from eval cases, fine tuning on logs that contain eval inputs, generating reference answers with the same model I'm testing, and calibrating a judge on the test split. So I keep a held out split that's used rarely and never for tuning, dedupe eval cases against any training or few shot pool, tag every case's provenance, keep adding fresh production cases, and check that offline trends still match online outcomes.
must_mention: few shot examples from eval cases
references from the system under test
held out split and provenance tags

followups.q: What is the system level analogue of a judge's dev and test split?
followups.a: Tune prompts on a dev portion of the golden set and report on a held out test portion run rarely.

traps: Reporting the pass rate on the same cases used to tune the prompt.

topic: Agent benchmarks and long horizon tasks
q: What is SWE-bench, and how are its tasks graded?
plain: SWE-bench gives a model a real GitHub issue, such as a bug report, together with the full code repository, and asks it to produce a code change that fixes the issue. The change is graded by running tests: the tests the real fix made pass must now pass, and the project's other existing tests must still pass. It has 2,294 tasks from 12 popular Python projects. When it was introduced in 2023, the best model, Claude 2, solved only 1.96 percent of them.
deep: Jimenez et al. (ICLR 2024). Construction: about 90,000 PRs from 12 Python repositories, filtered to merged PRs that resolve an issue and change test files, then to instances with at least one **fail to pass** test (failing before, passing after the reference fix) and no install or runtime errors: 2,294 tasks. Input: issue text (195 words on average) plus codebase (about 3,010 non test files on average). Output: a patch applied with unix patch; resolved if it applies and the task's tests pass, including existing tests (median 51 additional) that guard prior behaviour. Reference fixes edit 1.7 files, 3.0 functions and 32.8 lines on average. Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval resolved 1.96 percent in the paper. A 300 task Lite subset exists, and the human validated SWE-bench Verified is what Anthropic's agent post reports against. Continually updatable from new issues, which helps against contamination.
say: SWE bench gives the model a real GitHub issue and the whole repository and asks for a patch. It's graded by execution: the patch must apply, the fail to pass tests, which the original fix turned from failing to passing, must now pass, and the project's existing tests, a median of fifty one per task, must still pass. It has 2,294 tasks from twelve Python repositories, and reference fixes touch about 1.7 files and thirty three lines on average. In the 2023 paper, Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval solved just under two percent. There's a three hundred task Lite subset and a human validated Verified subset.
must_mention: fail to pass tests plus existing tests

followups.q: What is a fail to pass test?
followups.a: A test that fails before the reference fix and passes after it, showing the issue was resolved.

traps: Describing SWE-bench as function level code completion like HumanEval.

topic: Agent benchmarks and long horizon tasks
q: What is tau-bench, and how does it grade an agent?
plain: tau-bench puts an agent in a customer service conversation with a simulated customer, played by a language model, plus a database the agent can query and change through tools and a written company policy it must follow. There are two settings: a retail shop with 115 tasks and an airline with 50. At the end, the grader compares the final database with the correct target state and checks that the agent told the customer the required facts. For example, a correct return must change exactly the right order with the right payment method, however the conversation went.
deep: Yao, Shinn, Razavi and Narasimhan (2024). Each task is a POMDP with database state hidden behind API tools, a domain policy document, and a user simulated by gpt-4-0613 from a hidden instruction that guarantees one valid outcome. Retail: 500 users, 50 products, 1,000 orders, 7 write and 8 non write tools. Airline: 500 users, 300 flights, 2,000 reservations, 6 write and 7 non write tools. Reward $r = r_{action} \times r_{output} \in \{0,1\}$: final database identical to the annotated goal state, and required outputs present in the agent's messages. Necessary but not sufficient: an agent could act without the confirmation the policy requires. Results (2024): gpt-4o function calling about 61 percent pass hat 1 on retail and about 35 percent on airline. Evaluate both outcome (final state) and trajectory (policy compliance, tool call accuracy, steps) for your own agents.
say: tau bench tests tool using agents in customer service conversations. The agent gets database tools, a written domain policy, and a user simulated by GPT 4 from a hidden instruction, in a retail domain with a hundred fifteen tasks and an airline domain with fifty. Grading compares the final database with the annotated goal state and checks the agent told the user the required facts, so many different conversations can succeed. In 2024 GPT 4o with function calling scored about sixty one percent on retail and thirty five on airline. The paper notes a correct final state is necessary but not sufficient, since the agent might skip a required confirmation.

topic: Agent benchmarks and long horizon tasks
q: Define pass@k and pass hat k, and work an example.
plain: Both run each task several times. pass@k asks: in k tries, does at least one succeed? pass hat k asks: in k tries, do all of them succeed? A task solved 6 times out of 8 always includes a success in any 4 of those tries, so its pass@4 is 1.0, but all 4 succeed only about 21 percent of the time, so its pass hat 4 is 0.214. pass@k fits settings where something like a test suite picks the winning try; pass hat k fits customer facing agents, where every try is seen by a user.
deep:
From $n$ trials with $c$ successes per task, unbiased estimators (tau-bench paper):
$$\text{pass}^k = \mathbb{E}_{\text{task}}\left[\frac{\binom{c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right], \qquad \text{pass@}k = 1 - \mathbb{E}_{\text{task}}\left[\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right]$$
Example $n = 8$, $c = 6$: pass hat k for k = 1, 2, 4, 8 is 0.75, 0.536, 0.214, 0.0; pass@k is 0.75, 0.964, 1.0, 1.0 (computed). $\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$ is unbiased for $p^k$ when $c \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, p)$ (a simulation gave 0.317 against $0.75^4 = 0.316$). tau-bench: gpt-4o's retail pass hat 8 fell below 25 percent though pass hat 1 was about 61 percent. Reliability matters for agents in front of customers; pass@k matters when a verifier selects among attempts (CME295 Lecture 6 covers pass@k for reasoning).

```python
from math import comb
pass_hat = lambda n, c, k: comb(c, k) / comb(n, k)
pass_at = lambda n, c, k: 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)
print([round(pass_hat(8, 6, k), 3) for k in (1, 2, 4, 8)])   # [0.75, 0.536, 0.214, 0.0]
```
say: Both come from running each task n times and counting c successes. pass at k is the chance at least one of k attempts succeeds, one minus C of n minus c choose k over C of n choose k. pass hat k, from tau bench, is the chance all k succeed, C of c choose k over C of n choose k, averaged over tasks. For a task solved six of eight times, pass at four is one, but pass hat four is about 0.21. pass at k fits when a verifier picks the winning attempt; pass hat k fits customer facing agents, where every attempt is someone's experience. GPT 4o's retail pass hat eight was under a quarter.
must_mention: pass@k: at least one of k succeeds
pass hat k: all k succeed

followups.q: Why use the combinatorial estimator instead of (c/n) to the k?
followups.a: It is unbiased for p to the k from a finite sample of n trials; the plug in estimate is biased.

traps: Reporting pass@k for an agent whose every attempt reaches a customer.

topic: Agent benchmarks and long horizon tasks
q: How are long horizon agent capabilities measured, and how should you evaluate your own agents?
plain: One approach, from the research group METR, measures how long a task, timed by how long it takes a skilled human, a model can complete with 50 percent and 80 percent reliability. As covered in Stanford's CS329A, that length has roughly doubled every seven months, from seconds for GPT-2 in 2019 to nearly an hour for Claude 3.7 Sonnet in 2025. Another, OpenAI's GDPval, compares model work with professionals' work across 44 occupations. For your own agents, you grade both the final result and the path taken, run each task several times, and read the transcripts.
deep: METR time horizon (CS329A Part 8): fit success probability against human task duration across suites (HCAST, SWE-bench, RE-Bench) and report the duration at 50 and 80 percent reliability; reported doubling about every seven months from 2019 to 2025. GDPval: expert graded comparisons against professional work in 44 occupations across nine sectors, with win rates rising from 12.4 percent for GPT-4o to 47.6 percent for Claude Opus 4.1 (2025). Deep Scholar Bench evaluates generated literature reviews on synthesis, retrieval and citation verifiability. Own agents: outcome metrics (final state, task success, cost per success), trajectory metrics (tool call accuracy, policy compliance, steps, loops, escalations), multiple trials with pass hat k, slices by task length, and transcript review, since two agents with equal success rates can fail in different ways.
say: METR's time horizon method measures the length of task, in human working time, that a model completes at fifty and eighty percent reliability, and CS329A covers their finding that it has roughly doubled every seven months, from seconds for GPT 2 to nearly an hour for Claude 3.7 Sonnet in 2025. GDPval instead compares model work with professionals across forty four occupations. For my own agents I'd measure outcomes, final state, success and cost per success, and the trajectory, tool call accuracy, policy compliance, steps and loops, run each task several times for pass hat k, slice by task length, and read transcripts, because equal success rates can hide very different failures.
must_mention: task length at 50 and 80 percent reliability

followups.q: Why report the 80 percent horizon as well as 50?
followups.a: Deployment needs reliability; the horizon at 80 percent is much shorter than at 50.

traps: Evaluating an agent only on final answers from a single run per task.

q: What should you trace and monitor in an LLM application?
plain: Record a trace for every request, with one entry per step: the rewritten query, what retrieval returned and with what scores, each model call with its prompt version, each tool call with its inputs and outputs, plus tokens, time and cost for each. When something goes wrong you replay the trace instead of guessing. On dashboards, watch latency including the slowest requests, time to first token, cost per request and per solved task, how often retrieval comes back empty, refusal and guardrail rates, and the judge pass rate on sampled traffic. Remove personal data from traces, since they copy everything users said.
deep: Span per step (rewrite, retrieve, rerank, LLM call, tool call, verification) with inputs, outputs, retrieved ids and scores, prompt and model versions, tokens, latency, cost, errors. Standard tooling such as OpenTelemetry works; the MCP docs point new servers to OpenTelemetry or stderr for logging. Dashboards: p50, p95, p99 latency; time to first token; tokens and cost per request and per resolved task; empty retrieval rate; refusal rate; guardrail trigger rate; loop and budget stop rate; judge pass rate on sampled traces. Alerts on shifts. Privacy: redact personal data, control access, set retention; Anthropic's research team monitored decision patterns without reading conversation contents. Hamel Husain: searchable, filterable traces are the base of both evals and debugging.
say: Every request gets a trace with a span per step: the rewritten query, retrieval results with ids and scores, each model call with prompt and model versions, each tool call with arguments and outputs, and tokens, latency and cost per span. OpenTelemetry style tracing works fine. On dashboards I watch p50, p95 and p99 latency, time to first token, cost per request and per resolved task, empty retrieval rate, refusal and guardrail rates, loop or budget stops, and judge pass rate on sampled traffic, with alerts on shifts. Traces copy everything users say, so I redact personal data and control access.
must_mention: tokens, latency and cost per span
latency percentiles, cost per task, refusal rate

followups.q: Why cost per resolved task rather than per request?
followups.a: Cheap requests that fail and get retried can cost more per solved problem than a pricier model that succeeds first time.

traps: Logging only the final answer.

q: How do you hit a latency target and keep token spend bounded?
plain: Treat latency as a budget split across steps. For an 800 millisecond target, you might allow about 100 for query rewriting, 50 for search, 150 for reranking a short list, and the rest for the model to start answering, then measure each step's share. Common levers are running searches and independent tool calls at the same time, reranking fewer candidates, streaming the answer as it is written, and keeping the long fixed part of the prompt identical so it can be cached. Token spend gets hard caps: how many chunks go in the prompt, how many steps an agent may take, and how much a single task may cost.
deep: Latency: per stage budgets with p95 targets (an 800 ms end to end example comes from an interview prep write up); parallel retrieval and parallel independent tool calls; rerank depth as a knob (BEIR: about 450 ms to rerank 100 on a V100); smaller or distilled rerankers; streaming to cut perceived latency (time to first token); stable cacheable prefixes; avoiding sequential LLM calls where one suffices. Token budgets: top k times chunk size caps context; history compaction; max steps and tool calls; per task spend limits that trigger escalation instead of silent overspend (OWASP LLM10 unbounded consumption); effort scaled to query complexity. Measure each stage's p95 contribution, since the slowest stage dominates tail latency.
say: I treat latency as a budget per stage. For an eight hundred millisecond target, maybe a hundred for rewriting, fifty for retrieval, a hundred fifty for reranking a short list, and the rest until the first token, then I measure each stage's p95, because the slowest stage dominates the tail. Levers: parallel retrieval and parallel tool calls, fewer rerank candidates or a distilled reranker, streaming, a stable prefix so caching applies, and no extra sequential calls. For tokens I cap context at top k times chunk size, compact history, cap agent steps, and set a per task spend limit that escalates rather than silently overspending.
must_mention: caps on context, steps and spend

followups.q: What improves perceived latency without changing total time?
followups.a: Streaming tokens so the first words arrive quickly.

traps: Optimising average latency while p99 is dominated by one slow stage.

q: What kinds of caching help LLM applications, and what are the risks of semantic caching?
plain: Prompt caching stores the processed form of a long, repeated prompt prefix, such as instructions and documents, so later requests reuse it; Anthropic reported more than 2x lower latency and up to 90 percent lower cost for long cached prompts. Exact response caching returns a saved answer for an identical request. Semantic caching returns a saved answer when a new question is merely similar to an old one, which saves more but can be wrong: 'refund for monthly plans' might get the stored answer about annual plans. It can also serve stale answers or leak one user's answer to another user with different permissions.
deep: Tiers, cheapest first: prompt (prefix) caching reuses computation for a repeated prompt prefix; keep stable content (system prompt, tool definitions, long documents) at the front and variable content at the end (Anthropic 2024: more than 2x latency reduction, up to 90 percent cost reduction). Exact response cache keyed by normalised request plus versions. Semantic cache keyed by query embedding with a similarity threshold: risks are false hits on near paraphrases with different meaning (negation, different entity, different plan), staleness, and cross permission leakage; mitigations are scoping by permission set and tenant, TTLs and invalidation on document changes, conservative thresholds tuned on labelled query pairs, and excluding personal queries. Embedding and retrieval caches for popular queries.
say: Cheapest first: prompt caching reuses the computed prefix of a long, repeated prompt, so I keep the system prompt, tools and long documents at the front, and Anthropic reported over two times lower latency and up to ninety percent lower cost for long cached prompts. Then exact response caching for identical requests. Semantic caching returns a stored answer when a new query embeds close to an old one, which saves more but can answer the wrong question, refund for monthly served the annual answer, serve stale content, or leak an answer across users with different permissions. So I scope it per permission set, add time to live and invalidation, and tune the threshold on labelled query pairs.
must_mention: scope by permissions, TTL, tuned threshold

followups.q: What invalidates a cached answer?
followups.a: A change to any document it relied on, a model or prompt version change, or its time to live expiring.

traps: A global semantic cache shared across tenants.

q: How much can routing to a smaller model save, and what makes it safe?
plain: Routing sends easy requests to a small, cheap model and only hard ones to a large model. If 70 percent of traffic can go to a model one tenth the price, total cost falls to 0.7 times 0.1 plus 0.3 times 1, which is 0.37 of the original, a 63 percent saving. The saving is only real if the small model handles that 70 percent well, so you measure quality per route and track how often the router sends a hard question to the small model. A cascade is a safer variant: try the small model first and escalate when a check on its answer fails.
deep: Blended cost $= f \cdot r + (1 - f)$ relative to all large, with $f$ the share routed small and $r$ the price ratio: $0.7 \times 0.1 + 0.3 \times 1 = 0.37$. Anthropic's routing pattern sends easy questions to a small model (their example names Claude Haiku 4.5 versus Sonnet 4.5). CS329A Part 9 presents intelligence per watt results in which local models of 20B parameters or fewer handled 88.7 percent of real chatbot queries. Safety: a router evaluated on a labelled set (confusion matrix by difficulty), quality per route on the golden set, misroute monitoring in production, and cascades (small first, escalate on verifier failure or low confidence), whose cost includes the wasted small call on escalated requests: cost $= 1 \cdot r + e$ where $e$ is the escalation share.
say: With a router sending seventy percent of traffic to a model a tenth the price, cost is 0.7 times 0.1 plus 0.3 times one, so thirty seven percent of the all large baseline, a sixty three percent saving. CS329A even presents results where local models under twenty billion parameters handled most real chatbot queries. But the saving only counts if quality holds, so I evaluate the router's confusion matrix on labelled requests, track golden set quality per route, and monitor misroutes. A cascade is the safer variant, small model first, escalate when a verifier or confidence check fails, though escalated requests pay for both calls.
must_mention: blended cost f times r plus 1 minus f

followups.q: What does a cascade cost?
followups.a: The small call on every request plus the large call on the escalated share.

traps: Claiming routing savings without measuring the small model's quality on its share of traffic.
